title: Determine whether the individual is subject to the Army Act
body: Does the Army Act apply to this person and this event? The starting question is personal and temporal applicability. Do not assume that all contractors, family members, retired personnel, civilians or personnel of another service are subject to Army disciplinary jurisdiction. Identify service status, attachment, active-service context and relevant statutory category. Army Act s 2, s 3 ['Record service number, rank, unit, service status, attachment and relevant dates.', 'Read the precise clause of s 2 before selecting any offence or procedure.', 'Where inter-service employment is involved, test the 2023 Act and applicable authorising orders.', 'Seek JAG opinion if applicability is disputed.']

title: Distinguish statute, rule, regulation, order and editorial note
body: Which instruction prevails when references conflict? Use the hierarchy of binding legal authority. A rule must trace to statutory authority; an internal administrative instruction cannot override the Act or a binding judicial ruling. The notes printed in an annotated PDF are useful study aids but do not become law merely by appearing beside the rule. Constitution / Army Act / statutory rules / valid orders ['Identify instrument type, issue authority, effective date and amendment.', 'Check conflict against higher-level authority.', 'Label extracted editorial notes separately from enacted text.', 'Escalate unresolved conflict to the legal branch.']
references: Constitution / Army Act / statutory rules / valid orders [{'source_id': 'SRC-AA', 'locator': 's 191; legal foundation'}, {'source_id': 'SRC-AR', 'locator': 'Cover / notes under rules'}]

title: CO summary punishment: statutory entry point
body: Can I award a punishment without a court-martial? Section 79 recognises punishments without court-martial as specified in ss 80, 83, 84 and 85. Section 80 provides a particular category of powers concerning persons other than officers, JCOs and warrant officers; subject-matter, rank, authority and statutory restrictions must all be checked before exercising it. Army Act ss 79–82; Army Rule 22 ['Determine rank and category of accused at relevant time.', 'Identify competent authority and punishment permitted for that category.', 'Complete hearing process under AR 22 or document any legally available exception.', 'Check s 81 limits and other applicable restrictions; obtain review where doubt exists.', 'Record the award in the prescribed manner.']

title: Limitations on summary punishments
body: Can multiple punishments be combined? The Act prescribes types of punishment and limits on cumulative awards, including rank-dependent exclusions. Section 81 specifically addresses limits and combinations. A decision-support application must not output an award amount or duration without checking rank, action, relevant conditions and current empowered authority. Army Act ss 80–82 ['Read all operative subsections of ss 80–82, not an isolated list.', 'Check rank at commission of alleged offence and at punishment.', 'Check whether combining penalties is allowed and aggregate ceilings.', 'Check applicable prescribed scales and delegated competence.']

title: Hearing of charge under Rule 22
body: What do I do when an allegation is reported? Ordinarily every charge against a person subject to the Army Act must be heard by the CO in the presence of the accused, with an opportunity to cross-examine witnesses and present defence. Rule 22(1) includes a specific discretion to dispense with that sub-rule where the charge arises from a Court of Inquiry with Rule 180 compliance. Outcomes in r 22(3) include summary disposal, referral, written evidence, or (within scope) summary court-martial; conditions must be read in full. Army Rule 22 ['Verify identity and Act applicability; frame particulars precisely.', 'Place available evidence and witnesses before the competent CO.', 'Afford participation, questions and defence rights unless an express exception is correctly applicable.', 'Record reasoned disposal: dismiss / summarise / refer / reduce evidence to writing / authorised trial.', 'Record any reliance on the proviso to r 22(1) and evidence of r 180 compliance.']

title: Summary of Evidence under Rule 23
body: How is Summary of Evidence recorded? Where evidence is reduced to writing under r 22, r 23 covers taking witness evidence in the accused’s presence and hearing, opportunity to cross-examine, reading over/signatures, defence statement and witnesses. Statements should be accurately recorded and the prescribed language and interpretation safeguards observed. Special provisions govern absent or non-compellable witnesses. Army Rule 23 ['Appoint an appropriate recording officer under r 23.', 'Record all relevant prosecution and defence witnesses in prescribed sequence.', 'Record questions and answers, read over, obtain signatures or attestation.', 'Offer the accused the prescribed opportunity to make a statement and call defence evidence.', 'Apply interpretation/translation and document any exceptional evidence method.']

title: CO decision after Summary of Evidence
body: After SOE, what are the lawful options? The CO considers the evidence recorded under r 23 and chooses among the prescribed options: remand for court-martial, referral to superior military authority, or rehearing with dismissal or summary disposal where lawful. Where a court-martial route is selected, competence, referral requirements and timelines must be separately checked. Army Rule 24 ['Read the complete SOE, including defence material.', 'Assess whether an offence and requisite evidence are disclosed.', 'Record selected statutory route and its reasons.', 'Check authority before assembling any court-martial; make required referral and issue necessary warnings.']

title: Preparation for defence
body: What rights does the accused have before trial? Rule 33 protects preparation of defence, including confidential legal-adviser communication, witness access, and supply of material subject to its terms. Rule 34 addresses warning for trial. The precise timelines and possible modifications depend on type of court and active-service status and must be checked from the operative rule text. Army Rules 33–34 ['Provide applicable evidence and documents within the statutory period.', 'Ensure legal adviser and witness access as prescribed.', 'Check whether minimum warning period applies and record delivery.', 'Document any exception with express legal authority.']

title: Power to assemble a Court of Inquiry
body: When should a Court of Inquiry be convened? A Court of Inquiry (CoI) is an evidence-gathering mechanism, not a trial or an independent power to impose guilt. Rule 177 describes what it is, possible composition and assembling competence. Its exact membership, scope and need for additional orders require the facts, current regulations and JAG review. Army Rule 177 ['Define fact-finding question and purposes before convening.', 'Verify lawful convening authority and appropriate composition.', 'Appoint members and preserve independence/absence of conflicts.', 'Issue written terms of reference and relevant evidence preservation orders.']

title: Terms of reference and procedure
body: How detailed should CoI terms of reference be? Rule 179 directs the CoI to be guided by the assembling authority’s written instructions, which should fully specify the information required and whether a report is needed. The court can be reassembled as permitted by the rule and must forward proceedings to the authority who assembled it. Army Rule 179 ['Draft numbered questions of fact instead of a predetermined conclusion.', 'Define date, persons, incident, material and specialist evidence.', 'Specify whether opinion/report is sought and limits of remit.', 'Permit additional witnesses and record additional evidence lawfully.', 'Forward signed proceedings through authorised channel.']

title: Court of Inquiry and Rule 180 rights
body: What if a witness becomes potentially blameworthy during CoI? Whenever the inquiry affects the character or military reputation of a person subject to the Act, that person must have full opportunity to be present throughout, make a statement, give evidence, cross-examine witnesses affecting reputation and produce defence witnesses, subject to the express prisoner-of-war exception. The presiding officer must ensure meaningful notification and participation; where the issue emerges during evidence, adjourn and correct procedure. Army Rule 180 ['Monitor continuously whether any witness or line of inquiry affects someone’s character/reputation.', 'Serve notice explaining r 180 rights when triggered.', 'Give effective access to relevant witness examination and defence evidence.', 'Where prejudice emerges mid-inquiry, stop and arrange compliance before proceeding.', 'Record notice, participation, cross-examination and any declination.']

title: CoI evidence and later proceedings
body: Can CoI statements be used to prove guilt at court-martial? Rule 182 provides a general non-admissibility rule for CoI proceedings and statements against a person subject to the Act, with specified exceptions, including use for cross-examining a witness. Do not equate a CoI witness statement with admissible court-martial trial evidence. Review exceptions and the exact evidentiary purpose. Army Rule 182 ['Classify material as CoI record, independent evidence, or trial evidence.', 'If preparing disciplinary trial, collect admissible evidence independently where required.', 'Assess any proposed use of CoI material under r 182 proviso and applicable evidence law.', 'Seek JAG direction before using CoI admission as substantive proof.']

title: Court of Inquiry for illegal absence
body: What special rules apply after prolonged absence? The law provides special procedures for a CoI into illegal absence. Rule 181 prescribes oath or affirmation in defined circumstances; Rule 183 deals with required evidence and declarations. This is a distinct workflow requiring careful date calculations, inventories and contemporaneous records. Army Act s 106; Army Rules 181 and 183 ['Verify commencement and duration of alleged absence.', 'Follow statutory procedure for illegal absence and sworn evidence.', 'Reconcile unit records, kit records and communications.', 'Prepare prescribed declaration and register entries.']
references: Army Act s 106; Army Rules 181 and 183 [{'source_id': 'SRC-AA', 'locator': 's 106'}, {'source_id': 'SRC-AR', 'locator': 'rr 181, 183'}]

title: Copies of CoI statements/documents
body: Can a person obtain CoI evidence for his defence? Rule 184 addresses entitlement to copies of relevant statements and documents in CoI proceedings in specified circumstances, including when tried by court-martial. Assess the provision and any lawful restrictions before denying relevant defence material. Army Rule 184 ['Identify requester, proceeding status and relevant material.', 'Determine statutory entitlement, exceptions and restrictions.', 'Provide copies through authorised process and document acknowledgment.']

title: Jurisdiction and type of court-martial
body: Which type of court-martial is competent? The Army Act distinguishes forms and jurisdiction of courts-martial; jurisdiction turns on personnel, offence, convening authority, rank, and statutory limits. A generic chatbot should never select a court-martial solely from alleged misconduct label. Army Act ss 108–120 ['Identify offence and accused rank/status.', 'Read court-type rules, competent authority and exclusions.', 'Review applicability of s 120 for SCM and need for reference.', 'Have JAG review charge and forum before issue of convening order.']

title: Challenge and impartiality of court members
body: Can the accused object to court-martial members? Section 130 prescribes a challenge opportunity for members in specified courts-martial; objections and responses must be heard and recorded with the challenged member absent when adjudicating the challenge. Ranjit Thakur underlines the importance of this mandatory safeguard, impartial adjudication and review of disproportionate punishment. Army Act s 130; Ranjit Thakur (1987) ['Read the names of court members to accused as prescribed.', 'Ask for objections; record each objection and response.', 'Ensure proper exclusion of challenged member during determination.', 'Document the court’s decision and any replacement appointment.']
references: Army Act s 130; Ranjit Thakur (1987) [{'source_id': 'SRC-AA', 'locator': 's 130'}, {'source_id': 'SRC-RANJIT', 'locator': 'judgment discussion of s 130 and bias'}]

title: Court-martial petitions and statutory remedies
body: How can findings or sentence be challenged administratively? The Army Act provides petition routes against orders, findings or sentences of courts-martial and deals with annulment. Distinguish statutory petition requirements, confirmation stage, AFT rights, limitation and appropriate authority. Do not use a generic template without identifying the specific court and decision. Army Act ss 164–165 ['Identify court type, date, confirmation status and relief sought.', 'Identify applicable pre/post-confirmation petition route.', 'Collect full proceedings, findings, sentence and grounds.', 'Check subsequent AFT forum and time limits.']

title: Administrative termination versus disciplinary trial
body: Can an officer be removed without court-martial? Administrative termination and disciplinary prosecution have different legal bases, authorities and procedural safeguards. Rules 14–15 address specific types of officer-service termination. A commander must not assume that a charge which could not be proved can be automatically converted into administrative removal. Army Act ss 18–22; Army Rules 14–15 ['Define whether action concerns misconduct, inefficiency, medical grounds or other statutory basis.', 'Identify distinct competent authority and operative rule.', 'Verify notification, adverse material and reply rights; assess exceptions.', 'Obtain formal JAG/personnel-branch review before action.']

title: Civil offence and military jurisdiction
body: What if a serviceman commits an offence under ordinary criminal law? Section 69 provides for civil offences by persons subject to the Act, subject to statutory qualifications in s 70. Civil and military jurisdiction can interact; serious incidents also engage civilian reporting duties and contemporary criminal law. The legal team must assess the offence date and the applicable penal/procedural regime rather than rely on obsolete IPC/CrPC references. Army Act ss 69–70 ['Identify precise civilian offence and date of occurrence.', 'Determine service status, location, active-service context and statutory exceptions.', 'Notify and coordinate with competent authorities as lawfully required.', 'Seek JAG opinion before choosing forum or custody.']

title: Choice between criminal court and court-martial
body: Who decides the trial forum when both courts have jurisdiction? Section 125 identifies a specified senior military authority, or other prescribed officer, who may decide the forum where both criminal court and court-martial have jurisdiction. Section 126 provides a mechanism where a criminal court requires delivery of the person or reference for determination. This is not a discretionary election by the unit CO acting alone. Army Act ss 125–126 ['Confirm that both forums legally have jurisdiction.', 'Determine statutory deciding officer under s 125 and any valid prescription.', 'Preserve correspondence and coordinate with civilian authorities.', 'Follow s 126 process promptly upon judicial requisition.']

title: Discipline in inter-services organisations
body: Can a commander discipline personnel from another service? The 2023 Act and 2025 Rules address disciplinary authority and command/control within qualifying inter-services organisations. Determine whether the establishment and person are within statutory scope and whether specific designations or subordinate authorisations apply; do not simply transplant Army Act authority across services. ISO Act 2023; ISO Rules 2025 ['Verify organisation designation, command appointment and attachment order.', 'Identify the applicable parent-service law and cross-service powers.', 'Read the 2023 Act, 2025 Rules and any controlling appointment/notification.', 'Seek joint-services JAG review on unresolved competence.']

title: AFT service-matter jurisdiction and exclusions
body: Can this grievance be filed before AFT? AFT covers defined service matters and court-martial appellate matters. The definition in s 3(o) includes a wide range of conditions of service but expressly excludes categories such as transfers/postings, leave and certain summary court-martial matters. Jurisdiction must be determined using the exact exclusion text and current case law, not the label “Army grievance”. AFT Act ss 3(o),14–15 ['Classify claim against s 3(o) inclusions and exclusions.', 'Distinguish service application under s 14 from court-martial appeal under s 15.', 'Identify correct applicant, respondent, bench and relief.', 'Verify maintainability against later binding judgments.']

title: Exhaustion of remedies before AFT
body: Must statutory/departmental remedy be exhausted first? Section 21 says the AFT shall not ordinarily admit an application unless available service-law remedies have been availed. It also defines circumstances of a final rejection or expiry of six months without final action as satisfaction for this purpose. Do not turn the statutory word “ordinarily” into an unconditional bar. AFT Act s 21 ['Identify relevant statutory complaint/petition procedure.', 'Keep filing date, submission receipt and decision.', 'Compute s 21(2) threshold from actual record.', 'Have counsel assess exceptions and urgent relief.']

title: Limitation for AFT applications
body: How much time is available to approach AFT? Section 22 governs limitation for applications, including ordinary six-month periods under specified circumstances and a sufficient-cause provision. The date computation depends on the type of final order/representation, cause of action and later judicial interpretation. A legal assistant should show a provisional date only from verified inputs, and flag all exceptions for lawyer review. AFT Act s 22 ['Capture cause of action, statutory complaint, final order, and receipt dates.', 'Select correct limb of s 22; account for any relevant legal treatment.', 'Show timeline and source citation for the calculation.', 'Escalate late cases to counsel for condonation assessment.']

title: Appeal to Supreme Court and writ review
body: Can one challenge an AFT order before High Court or Supreme Court? Sections 30–32 establish a restrictive statutory Supreme Court appeal and leave framework. Parashotam Dass confirms that High Court jurisdiction under Article 226 to judicially review AFT decisions is not barred, while appropriate judicial restraint still applies. The remedy, deadline and merits must be assessed separately; writ review is not a routine unrestricted second appeal. AFT Act ss 30–32; Constitution Art 226; Parashotam Dass (2023) ['Examine impugned order, nature of dispute and governing appellate route.', 'If Supreme Court route considered, check leave requirements and statutory periods.', 'If writ review considered, assess constitutional review grounds and limits.', 'Seek counsel review of forum, maintainability and interim relief.']
references: AFT Act ss 30–32; Constitution Art 226; Parashotam Dass (2023) [{'source_id': 'SRC-AFT', 'locator': 'ss 30–32'}, {'source_id': 'SRC-PARASH', 'locator': 'paras 18,24–30'}]

title: Case-law method: Rule 180 is mandatory but effects are context-specific
body: Does any defect in CoI automatically invalidate a completed court-martial? The Supreme Court distinguished obligatory Rule 180 opportunity from the consequence of procedural defects at an earlier fact-finding stage. It held that in the facts of the case a CoI lapse raised only after full trial did not warrant a remand to conduct a fresh CoI, and discussed limits on AFT retrial/remand authority. Do not infer that a CO may disregard Rule 180. Virendra Kumar (2020) paras 12–16 ['Always ensure Rule 180 rights at the inquiry stage.', 'If alleged breach occurs, record when objection arose and whether cure is possible.', 'Separate procedural breach from remedy and identified prejudice.', 'Read full judgment and later treatment before legal opinion.']

title: Case-law method: impartial adjudication
body: What does Ranjit Thakur teach about procedural fairness? The judgment concerns court-martial composition, objection to members, actual/apparent bias and proportionality. It illustrates why mandatory court procedure and a fair adjudicating body are not technical formalities. Apply its ratio to factually comparable questions after checking subsequent authority. Ranjit Thakur (1987), s 130 ['Build a fact table and identify the precise challenge safeguard.', 'Distinguish legal ratio from surrounding commentary.', 'Check later authority on proportionality and court-martial review.']
references: Ranjit Thakur (1987), s 130 [{'source_id': 'SRC-RANJIT', 'locator': 'holding and discussion of s 130 / bias'}]

title: Case-law method: constitutional review of AFT
body: Does AFT extinguish High Court judicial review? The Supreme Court confirms that the High Court’s constitutional jurisdiction under Art 226 is not inhibited merely by the AFT framework; the High Court nevertheless exercises judicial restraint appropriate to military discipline and judicial review. Distinguish legal review from unrestricted reappreciation of facts. Parashotam Dass (2023), paras 24–30 ['Identify allegedly unlawful decision and constitutional review ground.', 'Check statutory AFT remedies and why further review is sought.', 'Characterise jurisdictional error, denial of rights or apparent error accurately.']

title: Standard record bundle for alleged misconduct
body: What documents should be preserved at the first report? Independent of eventual forum, preservation of contemporaneous evidence supports fairness and later review. Collect original records with custody and access logs while protecting confidentiality and ensuring that CoI material is handled under its separate rules. Evidence management; Army Rules 22–24, 177–184 ['Log first information, reporter and time.', 'Secure relevant correspondence, unit records, photographs, electronic evidence and witness contact information.', 'Maintain chain of custody; restrict access to authorised officers.', 'Seek JAG advice on disclosure, retention and admissibility.']

title: Escalation and stopping rules for commander assistant
body: When should a commander stop using the app and seek JAG? The assistant should provide source-grounded information, not certify guilt or authorise punishment. Mandatory escalation is prudent for serious or complex offences, arrest/custody, civilians or police, contested status/jurisdiction, Army Rule 180 objections, medical/mental-health concerns, contested evidence, SCM/GCM, dismissal/termination, appeals and any missing current order. Jurisdiction and natural-justice risk controls ['Show the relevant law and list missing facts.', 'Provide a documented issue brief instead of a dispositive instruction.', 'Mark any outcome as “Requires competent authority / JAG verification”.', 'Record reviewed version of law used.']

title: 1.1 Purpose and intended users
body: This volume is a working reference for commanding officers, presiding officers, members of courts of inquiry, adjutants, staff officers and JAG personnel. It concentrates on the legally distinct stages of incident reporting, fact-finding by a Court of Inquiry (CoI), protection of affected persons, preservation of information, review by the assembling authority, and transition to a separate disciplinary or administrative process. It is not a standing order authorising any individual action. All case-specific advice must be checked against the law in force on the event date, relevant service orders and delegated competence. ['Primary statutory material controls over a commentary, training note or application-generated answer.', 'Judgments interpret statutory provisions; identify the ratio, facts, subsequent treatment and exact paragraphs.', 'Administrative regulations and Army Orders may prescribe additional conditions; never invent missing text.', 'Treat generated specimen forms as editorial drafts until an authorised format is verified.'] []

title: 1.2 Source categories and legal force
body: The Army Act supplies the statutory basis. The Army Rules prescribe processes. Regulations for the Army and applicable Army Orders may impose incident-specific procedural or reporting requirements, but their current authorised editions must be obtained through service channels. Explanatory notes appearing under provisions in an annotated PDF are helpful, but must not silently be elevated to the legal force of the rule itself. Case law requires attention to both what the court decided and what it did not decide. ['The application should display a source hierarchy: Act > valid Rules > applicable regulations and orders > controlling judgment interpretation > JAG-approved commentary > unapproved study notes.', 'Store effective-from, effective-to, source version, acquisition route and amendment checks separately.', 'Where an authoritative source is missing or contradictory, the result must explicitly say verification is pending.'] []

title: 1.3 CoI compared with other proceedings
body: A CoI collects evidence and may be required to report on identified matters. It does not function as a court-martial. Hearing of charge under Rule 22, Summary of Evidence under Rule 23 and subsequent trial are legally different stages. A CoI finding should not be presented as a conviction or as an automatic substitute for a competent authority's decision. Supreme Court decisions have emphasised the fact-finding character of a CoI and the separateness of the subsequent trial. ['Do not frame guilt as conclusively established by a CoI.', 'Do not assume a CoI is invariably a prerequisite to a court-martial.', 'Do not treat all CoI witness statements as admissible substantive evidence at a trial: see Rule 182.'] []

title: 2.1 General fact-finding purpose
body: Rule 177 permits a CoI to be assembled to collect evidence and, if required, report on a matter referred to it. The rule itself does not state that every complaint, accident, stock discrepancy or misconduct allegation necessarily requires a CoI. Whether one is required for a particular incident may arise from a separate Act provision, another Army Rule, current regulations, an Army Order or a lawful superior direction. ['Record the factual event, date, unit, personnel involved and likely legal consequences.', 'Check for a specific mandatory CoI requirement instead of using Rule 177 as a universal mandate.', 'Identify whether evidence preservation or urgent protection of life/property must proceed immediately irrespective of the inquiry.'] []

title: 2.2 Absence without authority: special statutory inquiry
body: Section 106 sets out a special inquiry following a period of thirty days of unauthorised absence, including inquiry into relevant Government property deficiencies. Rule 183 prescribes recording of evidence and a declaration. Section 106 also prescribes entry of the declaration in the court-martial book and a consequence if the person subsequently neither surrenders nor is apprehended. This is a distinct statutory route: a generic incident-inquiry template is inadequate. ['Verify the dates precisely and exclude only such days as the applicable authoritative directions require.', 'Check whether the absence was without due authority or other sufficient cause; do not presume desertion merely from an initial absence report.', 'Verify statutory record-making, oath requirement and equipment inventory.', 'Review historical Rule 183 text concerning disposition of original proceedings against current retention and legal-hold requirements before taking any destructive action.'] ['Never instruct destruction of records from this training manual. Obtain the current authorised records instruction and preserve material subject to litigation or investigative hold.']

title: 2.3 Loss or theft of unit weapons: higher-authority route
body: Rule 185, as reproduced by public legal texts, contains a specific procedure when a weapon or qualifying part of a weapon forming part of unit equipment is lost or stolen in circumstances relating to Rule 186. It references an inquiry under orders of an officer commanding an army, army corps, division or independent brigade. This is not a routine CO-only convening situation. The exact modern command nomenclature, applicability, financial powers and current rule text require JAG verification. ['Immediately secure and report the event using the relevant security and armament instructions.', 'Check whether Rule 185 applies; refer convening competence to the formation authority rather than issuing a routine CO convening order.', 'Preserve issue/receipt and armoury records, access logs and contemporaneous witness accounts.', 'Do not recommend a collective fine without separate verification of Rule 186, evidence, authority and safeguards.'] ['Source-control flag: the full latest authenticated r 185/186 text is not yet included in the official-text package; these records are JAG-review mandatory.']

title: 2.4 Other commonly encountered incidents
body: Firearms accidents, vehicle accidents, training deaths, injuries, damage to military equipment, misuse of public stores, suspected financial irregularities and loss of sensitive records can call for inquiries. However, the precise trigger, convening rank, specialist membership, reporting time limit and additional forms depend on regulations or instructions that this public-source corpus has not yet authenticated. This volume therefore describes safe first actions and a verification checklist, not an invented single standing procedure. ['Separate urgent safety response and statutory civil reporting from the later fact-finding exercise.', 'Notify required specialist authorities under the current authorised standing orders.', 'Where allegations indicate a criminal offence, obtain competent legal advice on parallel military/civil processes.', 'Preserve evidentiary material before routine maintenance or reset.'] []

title: 3.1 Who may assemble the court
body: Rule 177(3) provides that a CoI may be assembled by the officer in command of a body of troops, whether from one corps or more. That general power must be read with any special rule that designates a different or higher authority. For example, the special weapon-loss procedure under Rule 185 should be checked before assuming routine unit-level competence. ['Identify assembling authority by appointment and current command, not rank alone.', 'Check special matters and current Army Orders for enhanced approval or reporting.', 'Record the exact legal basis and the assembling officer on the convening order.'] []

title: 3.2 Composition and impartiality
body: Rule 177(2) permits flexible membership including commissioned officers and specified junior ranks. A note in the annotated rules indicates that three members are normal; this note should not be confused with an inflexible statutory minimum. Composition must suit the facts and avoid real or reasonably apprehended bias. In Sanjay Jethi, the Supreme Court scrutinised persons whose prior role in preparing relevant material gave rise to a bias concern. ['Choose personnel with relevant technical understanding but no disqualifying prior commitment to the alleged conclusion.', 'Screen direct personal involvement, prior written adverse conclusions, supervisory responsibility for alleged lapses and personal conflicts.', 'Check whether a proposed member may later be disqualified from participating in a court-martial, with reference to Rule 39.', 'Preserve the recorded reasons for membership and any recusal or substitution.'] ['Do not confuse necessary technical expertise with impartiality; expertise does not cure prejudgment.']

title: 3.3 Written instructions are essential
body: Rule 179(1) requires the court to be guided by the written instructions of the assembling authority. Instructions must be full and specific, identify the general character of information required, and indicate whether a report is required. Vague terms such as investigate the matter and fix responsibility risk inviting conclusions beyond the evidence or masking the need to engage Rule 180 safeguards. ['Identify what occurred, where, when and which records must be examined.', 'Separate factual questions from any authorised opinions; keep conclusions open.', 'State whether findings and an opinion/report are sought and to whom proceedings are to be forwarded.', 'Clarify any technical scope, independent specialist assistance and records to examine.', 'Do not direct that a named individual be found guilty.'] []

title: 3.4 Example terms of reference (training draft)
body: A neutral ToR for a training-equipment incident could require the CoI to determine the verified chronology, equipment configuration before the event, custodian and access chain, contemporary documentation, tests conducted, and proximate circumstances. Any request to identify deficient procedure should be evidence-based and avoid a foregone conclusion. Where a person becomes adversely implicated, the court must consider Rule 180 rights at that stage. ['Establish chronology and location from independently identified sources.', 'Record inventory, issue/receipt, serviceability and technical records.', 'Identify relevant SOPs actually in force at the event time.', 'Record all material explanations, including exculpatory evidence.', 'State any factual uncertainty and records/witnesses not obtained.'] []

title: 3.5 Minimum convening-order data
body: An application-generated convening-order draft should record an authority, factual subject, appointment of presiding officer and members, location, scope and written instructions, whether an opinion/report is required, file or incident reference and how the proceedings will be sent. Rank and date are not a substitute for proving legal competence. Additional prescribed formats must come from current service publications. ['Identity and appointment of assembly authority', 'Evidence of special-rule approval where applicable', 'Names/roles of members, recusal check', 'Written terms and report requirement', 'Security classification and authorised document custody path'] []

title: 4.1 Opening conference and procedural record
body: At commencement the presiding officer should review the instructions and record that the membership understands scope, independence and any special evidence requirements. A contemporaneous proceedings log greatly assists later review. The presiding officer should ask whether the subject matter already affects the character or military reputation of any person subject to the Act, which determines whether Rule 180 must be actively implemented. ['Opening date and location; assembled members and any absence/substitution', 'Reference to the convening order and instructions', 'Witness schedule and material inventory', 'Initial Rule 180 screening for each potentially affected person', 'Record of procedural requests and orders of the presiding officer'] []

title: 4.2 Notice of sittings and adjournments
body: Rule 179(3) calls for previous notice of the meeting time and place and adjournments to all persons concerned, except a prisoner of war who remains absent. The precise circumstances and means of service should be documented. Where a person is engaged under Rule 180, meaningful notice should be sufficient to exercise the rights contemplated by that rule, having regard to the facts. ['Keep a dated notice and acknowledgment register.', 'Record any difficulty in contacting a person and the reasonable steps taken.', 'Consider adjournment when necessary to give an effective opportunity, rather than relying on a nominal notice.'] []

title: 4.3 Questions, witnesses and reassembly
body: Rule 179(4) enables the court to ask questions needed to test truth and accuracy and elicit facts. Rule 179(5) provides for reassembly on the assembling authority's direction for additional witnesses or further information. Rule 179(5A) includes a prescribed summons mechanism. An explanatory note to Rule 177 in an older official compilation says a CoI cannot compel civilian witnesses; how that note interacts with the summons rule and applicable statute must be confirmed by JAG, rather than treating a summons as an unlimited power over civilians. ['Record witness identity, service status, language and relationship to events.', 'Maintain question/answer and exhibits in logical order.', 'Use neutral questions before testing inconsistencies.', 'Maintain formal direction and dates for any reassembly.', 'Seek JAG review before treating any civilian witness as subject to compulsion.'] ['Witness compulsion is jurisdiction-sensitive. The application must show an explicit JAG-verification stop in civilian-witness cases.']

title: 4.4 When to take evidence on oath
body: Under Rule 181, witness evidence is recorded on oath or affirmation for prisoner-of-war inquiries, inquiries into illegal absence under Army Act Section 106, or other cases when the assembling officer directs. The members themselves ordinarily are not sworn under Rule 178, subject to the particular prisoner-of-war declaration identified in that rule. Do not assume every CoI witness must be sworn or that no CoI witness may be sworn. ['Check inquiry category and any written direction before the first witness.', 'Record the oath/affirmation or reason why it is not required.', 'Preserve the authorised form and language of the oath.'] []

title: 4.5 Recording reliable evidence
body: The rules establish core inquiry powers but do not provide an exhaustive modern digital-forensic protocol in the passages reviewed. A strong practice record distinguishes witness recollection, physical exhibits, system logs and expert inference. Capture the provenance of evidence and minimise undocumented alteration. Technical assertions should be supported by original logs, configuration records or specialist tests, not conclusory opinions. ['Use an exhibit register with original source, custodian, collection date/time and hash when appropriate.', 'Separate first-hand facts from hearsay and assumptions.', 'Record exculpatory documents and unresolved inconsistencies.', 'Maintain an audit trail when evidence is copied or translated.', 'Do not upload service-sensitive or classified data to an unauthorised cloud service.'] []

title: 4.6 Civil authorities, safety incidents and parallel processes
body: An incident may simultaneously raise service, criminal, safety, compensation and technical-investigation issues. Assembling a CoI does not displace a lawful civil investigation or decide whether an offence belongs before a civil court or court-martial. When civilians, a death, suspected serious crime, data loss or classified equipment are involved, the commander should identify parallel reporting obligations under competent orders and obtain legal advice without delay. ['Identify whether the location and participants trigger civil-police reporting.', 'Preserve potentially relevant material and protect witnesses from interference.', 'Avoid making promises of confidentiality beyond law or authorised policy.', 'Seek jurisdiction and evidence-handling advice before disciplinary action.'] []

title: 5.1 Legal trigger: reputational effect, not a formal charge alone
body: Rule 180 is engaged where an inquiry affects the character or military reputation of a person subject to the Army Act, save for the specified absent prisoner-of-war exception. The trigger depends on the effect of evidence and the nature of inquiry; it is not confined to a situation where a charge sheet has already been drafted. It may arise at inception or after an apparently neutral witness implicates an officer or soldier. ['Screen the subject matter before convening and after each material witness/exhibit.', 'Treat more than one person as potentially entitled to safeguards where the evidence affects them.', 'Do not wait until the final findings to consider rights.'] []

title: 5.2 Rights specified in the rule
body: The person concerned must have the full opportunity contemplated by the rule: to be present throughout the inquiry, to make a statement, to give evidence, to cross-examine witnesses whose evidence in the person's opinion affects character or military reputation, and to produce witnesses in defence of such character or reputation. The presiding officer is responsible for ensuring an affected person who was not previously notified receives notice and understands these rights. ['Record when rights were explained and to whom.', 'Document the opportunities actually provided, not merely a printed certificate.', 'If the opportunity to examine an adverse witness cannot be given, record the reasons and seek authoritative guidance.', 'Distinguish a voluntary waiver after meaningful opportunity from an opportunity never offered.'] []

title: 5.3 Mid-inquiry identification: practical response
body: The official annotated rules note that, when adverse material appears during a sitting, the presiding officer should arrange to afford the person Rule 180 facilities, including adjournment where necessary. Whether previously recorded material needs to be recalled or a reassembly is required depends on the evidence and ability to provide genuine cross-examination. A fresh notice alone does not repair an absence of meaningful participation. ['Identify the exact adverse statement or document.', 'Pause or adjourn where required to avoid conducting further consequential proceedings behind the person.', 'Provide the person a clear explanation of the issues and rights.', 'Plan lawful recall of relevant witnesses or further evidence where necessary.', 'Record what was revisited and what remains untested.'] ['An application cannot certify compliance simply because a notice template was generated.']

title: 5.4 Multiple affected people and competing rights
body: One event may affect several individuals who offer competing explanations. Each eligible person's opportunity must be considered distinctly. Membership must be independent of existing disputes and the court should avoid allowing one person's preferred narrative to become an assumption in the examination of another. The record should show how each person was notified and heard without compromising lawful confidentiality and security. ['Use a separate Rule 180 matrix for each affected individual.', 'Log specific adverse witnesses/exhibits, not a generic complied/not-complied label.', 'Document conflicts over witness availability and requests for reassembly.'] []

title: 5.5 Rule 180 and the later hearing of charge
body: The proviso to Rule 22(1) permits the commanding officer to dispense with the procedure in that sub-rule where a charge results from a Court of Inquiry in which Rule 180 was complied with in respect of that accused. This is a conditional statutory power, not automatic substitution. An application must verify how the charge arose, which individual received which safeguards, whether current rule text and subsequent developments allow the course proposed, and the CO's reasoned election. ['Before considering the proviso, verify an actual CoI and the link between inquiry and charge.', 'Verify Rule 180 compliance in respect of the accused, not merely another witness.', 'Preserve records supporting the decision to dispense; do not silently mark Rule 22 as completed.', 'Other pretrial rules and rights continue to require independent examination.'] ['STOP: proposed dispensation from Rule 22(1) requires a fact-specific legal review.']

title: 5.6 Legal consequence of noncompliance
body: Sanjay Jethi strongly affirms meaningful participation and impartial CoI membership. Virendra Kumar holds that, when a Rule 180 objection is made at the framing-of-charge or Summary-of-Evidence stage, the authorities must rectify the procedural defect. It also rejected an AFT-ordered de novo inquiry after a completed court-martial on the facts before it where the objection was not raised at earlier stages. This does not make Rule 180 optional, nor does it yield an absolute proposition that every subsequent administrative action survives a defective CoI. Later case law must be researched for the precise context. ['Do not use the slogan every defect voids everything.', 'Do not use the opposite slogan a Rule 180 defect is harmless.', 'Ask: Which order is challenged? At what stage? Was objection raised? Was prejudice shown? What corrective opportunity was actually offered?', 'Escalate remedies and litigation risk to JAG.'] []

title: 6.1 Rule 182: CoI proceedings are not trial evidence against the person
body: Rule 182 sets limits on use of CoI proceedings, confessions, statements and answers against a person subject to the Act. The text contains specified exceptions, including a trial for wilfully giving false evidence before the CoI and a proviso allowing the prosecution or defence to use the proceedings to cross-examine a witness. Thus the evidence-collection value of the CoI and its evidentiary treatment at court-martial are different. ['Do not paste CoI testimony into a trial brief as if automatically admissible substantive proof.', 'Identify the exact purpose for which a statement is proposed to be used.', 'Preserve original independent source evidence for later lawful proof.', 'Seek trial counsel/JAG opinion on admissibility and exceptions.'] []

title: 6.2 Rule 184: copies and disclosure requests
body: As transcribed in public legal sources, Rule 184(1) gives a person subject to the Act who is tried by court-martial entitlement to relevant statements and documents in CoI proceedings for prosecution or defence. Rule 184(2) addresses statements and documents bearing on a person's character or military reputation and specifies an exception involving a written order of the Chief of the Army Staff. This does not create an unqualified right to every paper, every opinion or an entire CoI report in all circumstances. ['Record applicant identity, service status, provision invoked and requested documents.', 'Identify relevant statements and documents and the basis of relevance.', 'Escalate any restriction or proposed refusal for review of current Rule 184(2), confidentiality, security and authorised procedures.', 'Provide a written decision through the competent channel; do not let an AI system refuse a legal entitlement.'] ['Official available text extract ends mid-Rule 184; full authenticated current text must be loaded before operational automation.']

title: 6.3 Forwarding proceedings and action by assembling authority
body: Rule 179(6) requires the presiding officer to forward the whole proceedings to the officer who assembled the CoI. The officer receiving them should distinguish findings of fact from opinions, review scope compliance and Rule 180 safeguards, and decide which additional action is legally authorised. Further disciplinary, administrative, financial and technical actions are governed by distinct provisions and competent approvals; the inquiry itself should not be the sole asserted authority. ['Check convening and membership legality, terms of reference, evidence, affected-person safeguards and any dissent or untested material.', 'Separate matters requiring additional investigation from those sufficiently established.', 'Obtain JAG advice before adverse action when procedural objections or serious consequences arise.', 'Record the actual statutory/administrative authority for follow-up.'] []

title: 6.4 Reassembly or supplemental inquiry
body: Where an omission or new evidence is discovered, Rule 179(5) permits the court to be reassembled as directed by the assembling officer to obtain more evidence. Reassembly should be clearly documented, with an audit trail of the earlier proceedings and subsequent instructions. It is not sufficient merely to generate a retrospective certificate that a person was heard if the contemporaneous record contradicts it. ['Record the deficiency or new matter prompting reassembly.', 'Issue a lawful direction and notify affected people as required.', 'Keep original material intact, appending supplemental proceedings rather than secretly rewriting testimony.', 'Re-evaluate findings after the added evidence.'] []

title: 6.5 Confidentiality, retention and disclosure control
body: CoI materials can contain personal, medical, classified and operationally sensitive information. The application should enforce role-based access, classification markings, purpose limitation and audit logs. The older text of Rule 183(3) contains an instruction about destroying original proceedings in the statutory absence inquiry; this cannot safely be converted to an app-wide automatic deletion rule without up-to-date legal and retention review, including any litigation hold. ['Retain versions and provenance; prevent silent amendment of signed proceedings.', 'Apply lawfully authorised retention schedules and preservation holds.', 'Separate access to legal headnotes from access to underlying classified facts.', 'Ensure offline deployment truly has no external document-upload path.'] ['STOP: archive, deletion and dissemination schedules require an authorised current records-management reference.']

title: 7.1 Illegal absence after thirty days
body: The special Section 106 process concerns proof of a thirty-day period of absence without due authority and recording relevant deficiencies. The court must examine sufficient witnesses and consider available witnesses on behalf of the absentee; an oath/affirmation is required. The Rule 183 declaration is reproduced in the court-martial book as directed. The application should present a dated absence chronology, not calculate desertion from an imprecise verbal report. ['Check day-one event, returns, permissions, hospitalisation and communications.', 'Verify lawful witness and proof requirements, including duty and attendance documents.', 'Review Government property chain and inventory separately.', 'Seek competent advice on return, surrender, apprehension and subsequent procedure.'] []

title: 7.2 Weapons or parts missing from unit equipment
body: A stolen or missing weapon is both an immediate security concern and, potentially, a special-rule inquiry. The text of Rule 185 ties the inquiry to orders of designated higher commanders. Rule 186 deals with potential collective fines, which are a distinct, highly consequential question. Nothing in this manual authorises a CO to impose such a fine or substitute ordinary fact-finding for the specific procedure. ['Take protective/security actions and make compulsory reports under authorised orders.', 'Verify item type, custody, armament numbers, last reconciliation and access records.', 'Identify if Rule 185 applies and identify correct formation-level authority.', 'Do not fix liability on an entire subunit without independently verifying the conditions and evidence.'] []

title: 7.3 Prisoners of war and exceptional subject matter
body: The special rules for prisoner-of-war cases include an additional declaration by members in the circumstance specified by Rule 178, directed opinions under Rule 179(2), specific oath requirements under Rule 181 and a limited Rule 180 exception for a prisoner of war who is still absent. These are exceptional, fact-specific cases and must not be processed using generic accident or misconduct templates. ['Verify legal status and whether returned or still absent.', 'Apply special member declaration and witness oath as required.', 'Identify statutory decisions concerning pay, dependants and relevant service status as separate matters.'] []

title: 7.4 Cases involving another service or civilian
body: Where Navy, Air Force, civilian employees, contractors or foreign personnel are involved, first identify which person is subject to which legal regime. Command of a joint establishment does not, by itself, prove that all participants are subject to all Army disciplinary processes. If the 2023 inter-services legislation applies, its current notified rules and specific command designation need dedicated verification. ["Record each person's service status and relevant command/attachment order.", "Do not use Army Rule 180 as a blanket description of every civilian's rights.", 'Check local civil jurisdiction and arrangements for evidence sharing.'] ['STOP: cross-service jurisdiction and civilians require legal review before procedural directions.']

title: 8.1 Major General Inder Jit Kumar v Union of India (1997)
body: The Supreme Court described the Court of Inquiry as a fact-finding process distinct from later court-martial proceedings. It cautions against treating the CoI itself as a contested criminal trial. Its principle should not be misread as waiving express protections under Rule 180 when a person's military reputation is affected. ['Application label: precedent / Supreme Court / interpretive.', 'Research the particular fact pattern and whether subsequent case law qualifies the rule.'] []

title: 8.2 Union of India v Major A Hussain (1998)
body: The judgment, cited and explained in Virendra Kumar, discusses irregularities in earlier investigation and their relationship with a completed court-martial. A defect does not automatically become a jurisdictional nullity merely because earlier fact-finding was imperfect; the role of mandatory provisions and prejudice matters. ['Application must ask whether a mandatory rule was breached and whether prejudice was raised or shown.', 'Do not advise ignoring a procedural obligation on the theory that a later trial might cure it.'] []

title: 8.3 Union of India v Sanjay Jethi (2013)
body: The Supreme Court stressed meaningful and effective Rule 180 participation and examined apparent bias in the membership of a CoI. The case illustrates that a court of inquiry can be fact-finding in function while still carrying binding safeguards for an affected person. Neutrality is especially important where members have already assembled facts, prepared adverse reports or adopted fixed conclusions. ['Screen member prior involvement before convening.', 'Enable meaningful cross-examination and defence evidence where Rule 180 applies.', 'Document any recusal request and considered decision.'] []

title: 8.4 Union of India v Ex Sep Virendra Kumar (2020)
body: The Supreme Court synthesised earlier cases and addressed the legal consequences of Rule 180 noncompliance. It held that objections at the framing-of-charge or Summary-of-Evidence stages require authorities to rectify the defect. On the case facts, it rejected reopening from the CoI stage after a completed court-martial where the issue had not been raised earlier, and examined restrictions on AFT retrial/remand authority. The judgment has a precise procedural setting; it is not a blanket immunity for noncompliance. ['Record the stage at which a legal objection was raised.', 'Review whether corrective opportunity was available and meaningful.', 'Do not confuse an AFT remedy restriction with permission to breach Rule 180.'] []

title: 8.5 Col Sandeep Sharma v Union of India (Delhi HC, 2024)
body: The Delhi High Court record concerns a CoI followed by administrative/service consequences and disputes about proper Rule 180 opportunity, reassembly and access to material. It reinforces that the substance of participation and accuracy of the proceedings record matter. The precise ratio and current appellate status require review before being used as an operational binding precedent. ['Prioritise a contemporaneous record of what witnesses/documents were actually made available.', 'Do not accept a compliance certificate as a substitute for examining the proceedings.'] ['Review subsequent appellate treatment before relying on this High Court judgment.']

title: 8.6 Case-digest format for the database
body: Every digest should store court, title, neutral citation and law-report citation where verified, date, bench, case number, facts, issues, holdings, relevant paragraph numbers, outcome, contrary cases, later treatment, last review date and legal relevance. A citation alone is not a digest; the application must retrieve the passage supporting each proposition. ['Link propositions at paragraph level, not just document level.', 'Include negative treatment and distinctions.', 'Attach status: source verified / holding reviewed / JAG approved / update required.'] []

title: 9.1 Standard decision sequence for any suspected incident
body: For every inquiry-related question the application should run a five-layer gate: (1) personal and territorial applicability; (2) incident-specific mandatory inquiry or reporting; (3) competent assembling authority; (4) affected-person safeguards; and (5) outcome and evidentiary pathway. A failure at any gate should be made explicit, rather than inferring authority from a generic manual section. ['G1: Who and what? Rank/status, unit, date, location and incident facts.', 'G2: Must a particular inquiry or report occur? Test Section 106, Rule 185 and current service orders.', 'G3: Which authority can convene it and who may be members?', 'G4: What rights, oath, notice, evidence and disclosure conditions apply?', 'G5: What does the CoI establish and what separate action is contemplated?'] []

title: 9.2 Pause and consult JAG triggers
body: A safe command assistant must escalate serious legal questions rather than giving a confident but incomplete answer. Particular triggers include proposed denial of Rule 180 rights, contested competence, questions on civilian witness compulsion, retrospective cures, administrative sanctions linked to contested inquiry, military/civil jurisdiction, document withholding, arms loss special rules and expunging signed proceedings. ['Hold or flag the proposed legal action in the draft workflow; the application has no command authority.', 'Display the legal uncertainty and the documents needed for JAG review.', 'Allow factual evidence preservation and emergency safety action to proceed as lawful.'] []

title: 9.3 Operational checklists as evidence of process, not certificates of legality
body: Checklists support consistency only if each item is linked to supporting records: served notice, actual witness opportunity, a summons or order, signed evidence, a decision on a request or approved reassembly. A checkbox must not be treated as a conclusive compliance certificate. The underlying source and record must be available to the reviewer. ['Every checklist item should include done/not applicable/blocked plus evidence pointer.', 'Reason for not applicable must be recorded.', 'High-risk incomplete items force escalation.'] []

title: 10.1 Unit of knowledge and provenance
body: Each knowledge card must answer a single legal or operational question and cite exact rule clauses or judgment paragraphs. It should carry legal issue, jurisdiction scope, actor, trigger facts, required evidence, decision steps, legal caveat, priority, effective date, source URL, notes versus rule distinction and mandatory review status. Versioning must preserve earlier records for audit. ['Do not flatten source versions into one undated plain-text paragraph.', 'Store exact source locator and source-type classification.', 'Record whether the proposition comes from express text, a judicial holding or editorial practice.'] []

title: 10.2 Verified retrieval and response policy
body: The offline retrieval engine should first filter the user's question by date, service, subject and legal task. It should then retrieve applicable Act/Rule paragraphs, relevant judgments and approved commentary. Generation must be constrained to retrieved authority; when the search returns no verified authority, the assistant should decline to make an operative legal determination and supply a research checklist instead. ['Primary statute/rule citation required for procedural claims.', 'Judgment pinpoint required for legal principles.', 'Display conflicting authorities and later-treatment status.', 'Disclose that a result remains unreviewed by JAG.'] []

title: 10.3 Test suite and review gates
body: No module should enter service until legal editors approve the source corpus and adversarial test cases. Tests must include changes of rank or service status, a questioned statute date, an absent witness, disputed Rule 180 rights, a deliberately wrong citation, missing current Army Order and attempts to solicit premature punishment. A safe assistant must identify unknowns and route to the appropriate human authority. ['Test each answer for source relevance, locator accuracy and absence of invented powers.', 'Re-run tests whenever a source is amended or judgment treatment changes.', 'Review output confidentiality and air-gap integrity.', 'Use role-based approval: drafter, legal checker, JAG approver, release manager.'] []

title: 10.4 Limitations and research backlog
body: This volume intentionally does not assert a complete list of mandatory Courts of Inquiry for accidents, disability, classified-loss incidents or financial irregularities. An authenticated current Regulations for the Army edition, relevant Army Orders and detailed local standing instructions are needed. The official-hosted Army Rules document consulted appears to be an older compilation, so amendment trace and promulgation checks remain necessary before live deployment. ['Acquire current official source editions with lawful provenance.', 'Check Rule 184-186 and linked order/notification changes.', 'Confirm forms, mandatory retention and hierarchy of appeals.', 'Conduct review of case law after 2024 including 2026 decisions; record subsequent treatment.'] ['Release gate: entire Volume II remains JAG-REVIEW-PENDING and cannot be treated as operational legal authorisation.']

title: Scope of this volume and hierarchy of authority
body:
Military justice involves distinct preliminary, summary disposal and court-martial processes. An officer must establish both personal jurisdiction over the individual and legal authority for each proposed act. A study note does not confer any power.
Identify service status, rank at offence and present rank, unit and controlling commanding officer.; Identify offence alleged, date of act/knowledge and governing statutory section.; Select the legally available process; do not assume that a Court of Inquiry is a prerequisite.; Confirm the current orders, delegations and JAG directions in the unit holding.
Confusing a charge hearing with a trial; Treating explanatory notes as promulgated law; Assuming a CO may punish every rank

title: Preliminary triage: incident versus offence
body:
Not every operational failure, shortage or administrative disagreement amounts to an offence under the Army Act. Identify facts, an offence provision, and supporting evidence before selecting disciplinary procedure.
Preserve first information; separate witnesses from conclusions.; Identify each act or omission, possible statutory section and relevant mental/causal elements.; Consider urgent safety/security steps independently of culpability.; Where no statutory offence is disclosed, use the lawful administrative/safety channel, not a fabricated disciplinary charge.
Using Army Act section 63 for every irregularity without reason; Deciding guilt in a CoI; Blurring criminal and administrative remedies

title: Hearing of charge: nature and purpose
body:
Rule 22 provides a preliminary command hearing of a charge in the presence of the accused, with an opportunity to cross-examine adverse witnesses, call witnesses and make a defence statement. This is not a finding of guilt by court-martial.
Confirm a properly identified allegation before the CO.; Bring the accused before the CO and ensure understanding.; Make relevant adverse witness evidence available for examination under the rule.; Allow appropriate defence witnesses and statement; document genuine participation.; Record a reasoned decision as to the further lawful course.
Absence of accused without legal foundation; Token opportunity to cross-examine; Ordering Summary of Evidence before lawfully determining course

title: Rule 22(1) proviso after Court of Inquiry
body:
The CO may dispense with the Rule 22(1) procedure for a charge arising from CoI investigation when Rule 180 was complied with in respect of the accused. The proviso is not an automatic waiver of all later safeguards.
Establish that the charge actually arises from the identified CoI.; Inspect actual Rule 180 notice, hearing and cross-examination record for that individual.; Confirm a competent CO decision to rely on the proviso and document its basis.; Continue with the subsequent process under applicable rules.
Treating any CoI as sufficient; Backdating or assuming Rule 180 compliance; Treating the CoI finding as conviction

title: CO dismissal and prohibited dismissal
body:
Rule 22(2) directs dismissal if the CO finds that the evidence does not disclose an offence under the Act; it also permits dismissal where proceeding is inappropriate, subject to a special proviso requiring reference to superior authority for charges the CO is debarred from trying under Section 120(2).
Analyse facts against the alleged offence elements.; Identify whether Section 120(2) is engaged.; If the proviso applies, refer to competent superior authority instead of unilateral dismissal.; Record action and supporting reasons in the relevant authorised format.
Missing statutory offence; Unlawful dismissal of restricted charge; Confusing insufficiency of evidence with exoneration after trial

title: Four routes following Rule 22 hearing
body:
After a charge is heard and the CO finds that it should proceed, Rule 22(3) provides four possible procedural routes: summary disposal under Section 80, reference upward, reduction of evidence to writing, or SCM where lawfully permitted for personnel below warrant-officer rank.
Test the person’s rank and eligibility before considering Section 80 or SCM.; For summary disposal, verify authorised punishments, extent and Appendix III.; For further investigation, order Rule 23 record in accordance with competence.; For SCM, check Section 120(2) and need for prior reference.
Treating choice as automatic escalation; Ordering SCM against JCO/WO/officer; Ignoring prior-reference proviso

title: New offence emerging from the evidence
body:
Rule 22(4) permits suitable further charge(s) if evidence in the Rule 22 process discloses another offence. It does not authorise surprise punishment on an undisclosed allegation without applicable safeguards.
Identify exactly what new evidence indicates.; Draft and scrutinise any revised allegation against statutory elements.; Ensure the accused receives the applicable charge procedure before further disposal.; Preserve an auditable record of why the new offence was considered.
Changing charges without notice; Applying a criminal section retrospectively without factual basis

title: Summary of Evidence: ordering and scope
body:
Under Rule 23, evidence is reduced to writing following an adjournment under Rule 22. Evidence given before the CO, both adverse and favourable, and other relevant evidence is recorded in the accused’s presence and hearing before the CO or an officer directed by the CO.
Confirm that the CO ordered the Rule 23 stage.; Specify charge(s), officer recording and applicable stage.; Take down relevant witnesses for prosecution and defence.; Ensure accused’s presence, hearing and effective participation.
Officer taking SoE without CO direction; Ignoring defence witnesses; Treating SoE as sworn trial testimony

title: SoE cross-examination and questions/answers
body:
The accused may question each witness in cross-examination, and both the question and answer must be included in the recorded evidence. The recording officer must not filter away material questions merely because they are inconvenient.
Record the witness narrative and questions in the sequence followed.; Read over recorded statement to witness and obtain signature or compliant mark/witness attestation.; Record material corrections and dates transparently.; Preserve the accused’s opportunity to question the witness.
Paraphrasing away defence questions; Unsigned witness statements; Altering evidence after signature

title: Accused statement, silence and defence witnesses
body:
After adverse evidence, the accused is invited to make a statement but is not obliged to do so; any voluntary statement is recorded and read over. The accused is not cross-examined on that statement at this stage and may call defence or character witnesses.
Use the current authenticated caution, in a language the accused understands.; Record whether a statement was made voluntarily, without suggesting silence implies guilt.; Read over the statement and document corrections.; Allow relevant defence and character witnesses in accordance with the rule.
Coercing admissions; Treating silence as proof; Using an inaccurate caution copied from an OCR error

title: Language, interpretation and translation
body:
Evidence and an accused statement are recorded in English; when the witness or accused does not understand English, the recorded text must be interpreted into a language understood by that person.
Identify actual language comprehension instead of assuming English understanding.; Use a competent and impartial interpreter as required.; Read/interpret the recorded final version and allow corrections.; Record interpreter identity and any dispute.
Signing an English record the witness could not follow; Not recording translation dispute

title: Unavailable witnesses under Rule 23(5)
body:
A signed written statement may be included when a witness cannot be compelled to attend, or attendance cannot readily be procured for reasons expressly considered and certified by the recording officer. This is a conditional exception, not a blanket permission to replace all live testimony.
Establish the recognised reason for non-attendance.; Record written certification and its factual basis.; Read written statement to the accused.; Flag any cross-examination prejudice for the subsequent authority.
Form certification with no grounds; Using absence to suppress cross-examination; Treating SoE statement as automatically admissible substantive trial evidence

title: Civilian witnesses and statutory summons
body:
Rule 23(6) permits a non-military witness to be summoned by a CO order in the form prescribed by Appendix III. Actual powers, service requirements, and practical enforcement must be verified; a unit may not improvise coercive measures.
Check status and relevance of civilian witness.; Use current authorised Appendix III summons process.; Coordinate with JAG for service and enforcement if contested.; Preserve witness evidence and available documentary material.
Using unauthorised summons format; Assuming power to detain civilian witness

title: Rule 24: decision after Summary of Evidence
body:
The CO must consider the written Summary of Evidence and decide whether to remand for court-martial, refer the case to proper superior military authority, or re-hear and dismiss/otherwise lawfully dispose of the charge.
Read full SoE including defence evidence and statement.; Check offence, competence, jurisdiction, limitation and essential witnesses.; Record selected Rule 24 route and supporting reasons or referral.; If remanded for trial, avoid unnecessary delay and make requisite convening reference.
Automatic trial merely because SoE exists; Ignoring exculpatory evidence; Omitting superior reference

title: Army Rule 25: obsolete references
body:
The examined Army Rules text explicitly marks Rule 25 omitted with effect from the 1993 amending notification. Any older training paper requiring present-day Rule 25 process must be checked against current law rather than reused.
Scan every specimen and SOP for references to Rule 25 as an active rule.; Replace obsolete steps only after legal review of current law.; Preserve historical rule versions solely for cases to which they genuinely apply.
Applying historical officer-charge procedure today; Citing cancelled rule as live authority

title: Section 79 and summary punishment framework
body:
Section 79 recognises punishment otherwise than by court-martial through the specific statutory pathways. Section 80 primarily addresses persons other than officers, JCOs or warrant officers. Sections 83, 84 and 85 establish separately constrained authorities for officers/JCOs/warrant officers.
Determine rank and status exactly.; Determine competent officer for that rank and specific offence.; Check permitted punishment types, applicable caps and current delegated orders.; Apply prescribed procedure and record transmission or review rights.
One-size-fits-all punishment table; Assuming CO can reprimand officers under Section 80

title: Section 80: statutory punishments and limitations
body:
Section 80 specifies statutory punishments including custody, detention, confinement to lines, extra duty, specified deprivation, reprimand for eligible ranks, fine and penal deductions. Section 81 imposes rank and aggregate limitations. Section 82 permits other specified punishments only with the statutorily required Government consent.
Identify which clause is proposed and what ranks it legally covers.; Check Section 81 restrictions: e.g., custody/detention/confinement are not awardable to NCOs; reprimand is not for ranks below NCO.; Check ceilings, coexistence of multiple awards, and any notified additional punishments.; Complete the authorised record and applicable transmission.
Awarding NCO imprisonment in military custody under Section 80; Awarding severe reprimand to a sepoy; Improper aggregate days

title: Section 81: combining punishments
body:
Section 81 prescribes conditions on combined awards, including sequencing and a 42-day aggregate cap in relevant combinations. It also prohibits the Section 80(a)-(c) awards to persons who are or were NCOs when the offence occurred and reserves reprimand awards to eligible rank.
Check exact rank when the offence occurred and rank at award.; Map proposed combination to statutory clauses.; Compute periods explicitly, including any current punishments.; Record each section and administrative consequences.
Using current rank only; Ignoring aggregate cap; Awarding prohibited punishment type

title: Section 83: superior powers for officer/JCO/WO
body:
An officer holding powers not less than a brigade/equivalent command or another properly specified officer may deal summarily with an officer below field-officer rank, JCO or WO, with the remedies expressly listed under Section 83, subject to the prescribed procedure.
Check whether accused falls within Section 83 rank eligibility.; Verify authority’s actual statutory command status or designation.; Use Rule 26 safeguards and lawful charge procedure.; Transmit proceedings as required by Sections 86-88.
Assuming all brigadiers can punish all officers; Ignoring officer rank threshold; Skipping required 24-hour provision

title: Section 84: superior powers and election right
body:
An area/equivalent commander or other competent specified authority may apply Section 84 within defined rank limits. For forfeiture of seniority or qualifying service, Section 84(a) preserves the accused’s right, before award, to elect trial by court-martial.
Confirm officer rank and authority eligibility.; Identify proposed punishment precisely.; If clause (a) contemplated, document the statutory election opportunity before any award.; Use prescribed Rule 26 procedure and mandatory review route.
Omitting an election right; Confusing forfeiture with normal promotion policy; Exceeding 12-month cap under Section 84(a)

title: Section 85: CO authority for JCOs
body:
Section 85 provides a limited CO (or specified equivalent) summary route against a JCO. It lists severe reprimand/reprimand and stoppage of pay/allowances for proved loss or damage, with an express restriction on reprimand by an officer below Colonel.
Verify JCO rank and appointment of awarding authority.; Check that the contemplated punishment is one Section 85 permits.; Check Rule 26 procedural safeguards.; Record any proved loss and its evidential/quantum basis.
Awarding severe reprimand below Colonel rank; Using Section 80 against JCO; Unproven loss recovered as punishment

title: Rule 26: rights in summary disposal of officer/JCO/WO
body:
For a person remanded for superior summary disposal, the charge and Summary of Evidence must be provided without charge at least 24 hours before disposal. Unless the charge is dismissed or the accused consents in writing to dispensing with witness attendance, evidence is heard in the accused’s presence with full liberty to cross-examine and call defence witnesses.
Serve charge and Summary of Evidence with proof of time.; Record any actual written consent to dispense with witness attendance.; Hear relevant witnesses in the accused’s presence if required.; Record defence and forward prescribed proceedings with conduct sheet and SoE.
Presuming consent from silence; Serving late without documenting timing; Missing proceedings on forwarding

title: Sections 86-88: transmission and superior review
body:
Punishments under Sections 83-85 carry prescribed transmission obligations and superior review powers. A punishment may be scrutinised as illegal, unjust or excessive; the unit should ensure its paper trail and applicable channels are preserved.
Prepare authenticated proceedings, charge, SoE, conduct sheet and consents.; Identify the legally defined superior authority.; Transmit through the correct chain in the prescribed form.; Record any correction/review orders and execute lawfully.
Treating the award as beyond review; Not forwarding mandatory records

title: Summary Court-Martial is not summary punishment
body:
A Summary Court-Martial (SCM) is a judicial tribunal under the Act and distinct from Section 80 summary punishment. Its jurisdiction, trial procedures, confirmation/execution and appellate/review routes are not interchangeable with an ordinary CO disposal.
Check whether SCM is available for accused’s status and unit command.; Check Section 120(2) restrictions and reference exceptions.; Apply the court-martial trial safeguards rather than summary punishment form.; Seek legal advice on convening, evidence, sentence and remedies.
Using SCM as quick punishment; Trying a JCO/WO/officer by SCM; Ignoring statutory limits

title: Section 120(2) and prior reference before SCM
body:
Unless the statutory grave-immediacy exception applies, charges under Sections 34, 37 or 69 or an offence against the officer holding an SCM require reference to the competent superior court-martial authority before SCM. The exception must not be used as routine convenience.
Identify alleged offence section and victim/complainant.; Determine whether reference can be made without detriment to discipline.; Where required, make timely reference and retain written result.; If grave exception asserted, require contemporaneous legal and factual review.
Pretending every urgent case justifies exception; Trying Section 69 offence without required screening

title: Delay, limitation and expiry
body:
