title: Determine personal applicability
body:
Command question: Does the alleged offender fall under the Army Act?
Legal basis: Army Act ss 2-3
Legal position: Military jurisdiction begins with the statutory status of the individual on the relevant date. Serving soldiers, officers, attached personnel and persons whose liability survives cessation of service may require different legal tests. Uniform, physical presence on a defence establishment or employment by a contractor does not by itself establish subjection to the Army Act.
Assessment: Identify individual and service/attachment status; Confirm incident date and any discharge/retirement date; Read relevant sub-clause of section 2; Test whether another Service Act or inter-service framework governs; Seek JAG opinion on disputed status
Records: Service record; Attachment orders; Date-of-incident duty roster; Discharge records
Red flags: Assuming civilians or families automatically subject to Army law; Ignoring later termination of service
Illustration: Civilian contractor involved in a unit accident is not automatically subject to the Army Act.

title: Distinguish military offence from civil offence
body:
Command question: Is misconduct created by Army law or ordinary criminal law?
Legal basis: Army Act ss 3(ii),34-70
Legal position: Army Act sections 34-68 define military-specific offences. Section 3(ii) defines a civil offence by reference to an offence triable by a criminal court, and section 69 deems qualifying civil offences committed by persons subject to Army law to be offences against the Army Act, subject to section 70. The classification affects forum choice and procedure.
Assessment: Identify alleged conduct precisely; Identify possible Army-specific offence; Identify civil statute and date-specific offence; Screen section 70; Record overlapping legal routes without choosing a trial forum at unit level
Records: Incident narrative; Exact alleged acts; Statute text as on date; Rank/status confirmation
Red flags: Using generic disobedience language to replace an alleged civil crime; Assuming section 69 removes civilian jurisdiction
Illustration:

title: Section 69 reach and limitation
body:
Command question: Can a civil offence be tried by court-martial?
Legal basis: Army Act s 69 subject to s 70
Legal position: Section 69 is the statutory route by which a civil offence can, when charged under that section, be tried by court-martial if other requirements are satisfied. It is not a universal election by the unit. The underlying criminal offence, competent military trial, limitation, jurisdiction, and the other competent criminal court must be examined independently.
Assessment: Record substantive civil offence and penalty; Check law applicable on offence date; Apply section 70 restrictions first; Check competent military forum and procedural prerequisites; Ask authorised legal authority to assess concurrent jurisdiction
Records: FIR/complaint; Elements-of-offence assessment; Statute consolidation; Unit service-status proof
Red flags: Treating every allegation as eligible for SCM; Misreading section 69 as automatic bar on police action
Illustration:

title: Section 70 exception screen
body:
Command question: Can murder, culpable homicide or rape against a civilian be tried by court-martial?
Legal basis: Army Act s 70
Legal position: Section 70 ordinarily excludes court-martial trial of the stated offences against persons not subject to military, naval or air-force law. Its specified exceptions concern commission while on active service, outside India, or at a frontier post notified by the Central Government. These are statutory conditions, not descriptions of an ordinary unit posting.
Assessment: Identify victim status; Classify alleged offence accurately; Evaluate each expressly stated exception with documents; Check any Gazette notification for frontier post; Obtain JAG opinion and competent authority decision
Records: Victim status; Operations orders; Duty/status evidence; Location and notifications; Police case papers
Red flags: Calling a peacetime station active service without authority; Using section 70 to suppress allegations; Ignoring protected victim rights
Illustration: Alleged homicide of a civilian near a cantonment does not itself establish an active-service exception.

title: Concurrent jurisdiction is not exclusive immunity
body:
Command question: Can police and civilian courts deal with the incident?
Legal basis: Army Act ss 69,125-126; State of Sikkim (2022)
Legal position: The Supreme Court recognises that where a civil offence also falls within the Army Act, ordinary criminal courts and courts-martial can have concurrent jurisdiction. The Army Act does not grant blanket exclusion of ordinary criminal jurisdiction. The choice and adjustment process turns on statutory authority, procedural stage and the conduct of the competent military authority.
Assessment: Verify concurrent competence rather than assuming; Find procedural stage of civil proceedings; Locate any forum decision by authorised officer; Preserve written communications with Magistrate; Escalate forum conflict promptly
Records: FIR and charge sheet; Court notices; Authority decision; Court status notes
Red flags: Claiming military personnel cannot be tried in civil courts; Making forum choice through an unauthorised CO letter
Illustration:

title: Section 121 and double-trial screening
body:
Command question: Can the same offence be prosecuted twice?
Legal basis: Army Act s 121; constitutional safeguards
Legal position: Army Act section 121 contains protections against a second trial or punishment in specified circumstances. A related civil and military allegation is not automatically the same legally defined offence. Before beginning another proceeding, the competent authority must examine earlier conviction, acquittal or summary disposal, the identity of the alleged acts, and legal consequences.
Assessment: Record every prior court and service disposal; Identify legal offence and underlying conduct; Check whether first proceeding was final and legally competent; Seek legal analysis of second proceeding risk
Records: Prior judgments; Punishment book; Charge sheets; Disposal orders
Red flags: Equating administrative action with conviction; Beginning second prosecution without reviewing first
Illustration:

title: Cessation of military liability
body:
Command question: Can a retired soldier still be tried for an earlier offence?
Legal basis: Army Act s 123 and s 122
Legal position: Section 123 contains a continuing-liability mechanism for offences committed while subject to the Army Act, with strict statutory time and exception provisions. It does not make every retired person subject to unlimited military criminal jurisdiction. The ordinary criminal court jurisdiction must be separately considered for qualifying civil offences.
Assessment: Record precise service-cessation date; Identify alleged offence date; Check sections 122 and 123 and exclusions; Preserve any injunction or evasion date evidence; Refer to JAG for limitation and forum advice
Records: Retirement date; Offence chronology; Proceeding initiation; Court stay orders
Red flags: Assuming no military jurisdiction after retirement; Assuming unlimited post-service jurisdiction
Illustration:

title: Competent forum-choice authority
body:
Command question: Can a unit CO decide court-martial rather than civilian trial?
Legal basis: Army Act s 125
Legal position: Section 125 initially places the choice, where both courts have jurisdiction, with officers of specified higher command or another officer duly prescribed. A unit CO should not assume that his ordinary command appointment gives an independent section 125 power. Separate procedural roles of a commanding officer under adjustment rules must not be conflated with the statutory forum-choice power.
Assessment: Identify both possible jurisdictions; Identify and authenticate exact competent officer/warrant; Refer with facts and proceedings stage; Obtain recorded forum decision; Track communication to police/court
Records: Competent authority warrant; Recommendation note; Authority decision; Case diary
Red flags: Forum choice made by an officer without power; Oral or undocumented waiver
Illustration:

title: Section 126 reference to Central Government
body:
Command question: What if a competent criminal court insists on trial?
Legal basis: Army Act s 126
Legal position: When the court having jurisdiction issues the written requirement contemplated by section 126, the designated military officer must take one of the statutory routes: delivery to civil process, or prompt reference for Central Government determination. This is a formal jurisdictional mechanism; local agreements cannot override court directions.
Assessment: Receive and diarise court notice; Identify competent section 125 officer; Check statutory alternatives; Escalate to authorised authority without delay; Preserve any Government determination and comply
Records: Court requisition; Authority brief; Proof of reply; Government determination
Red flags: Ignoring court notice; Claiming Army automatically has final say; Continuing inconsistent parallel trials
Illustration:

title: 1978 adjustment rules: scope and status
body:
Command question: Which coordination rules apply between Magistrate and command?
Legal basis: 1978 Adjustment Rules; BNSS s 521
Legal position: The 1978 Rules prescribe a notice-and-adjustment mechanism when an accused subject to service law is brought before a Magistrate for an offence potentially triable by court-martial. They were framed under CrPC section 475, now broadly corresponding to BNSS section 521. Their continuing operation and any post-2024 adaptation require current Gazette/JAG verification before operational use.
Assessment: Establish whether Magistrate has case before him; Locate current authoritative rules; Compare transitional and adaptation instruments; Apply applicable notice mechanism after legal review; Record all dates and response deadlines
Records: Magistrate case status; 1978 rule copy; Current notification; Notice receipt and reply
Red flags: Treating historical CrPC citations as self-evidently current; Missing notice period; Assuming rules apply before a Magistrate is involved
Illustration:

title: Notice under 1978 Rule 4
body:
Command question: What should a unit do when a Magistrate notifies the CO?
Legal basis: 1978 Rules rr 3-4, subject to authentication
Legal position: The historical Rule 4 requires written notice before certain Magistrate actions and refers to a 15-day interval from service. Whether and how that period applies today must be confirmed against current valid instruments. Unit responsibility is to diarise notice, refer jurisdiction immediately and obtain lawful direction, not to ignore the criminal court.
Assessment: Check date and mode of notice service; Identify authority entitled to act; Send complete case papers immediately; Track any applicable restriction on Magistrate actions; Respond through approved counsel/authority
Records: Notice original; Service proof; Legal advice; Authority reply
Red flags: Waiting until day 15 to act; Unverified 15-day deadline in current matter; Unit CO claiming section 125 election
Illustration:

title: When Army has cooperated with civilian trial
body:
Command question: Can a unit later reverse its earlier civil-court cooperation?
Legal basis: State of Sikkim v Jasbir Singh (2022)
Legal position: Jasbir Singh addresses the significance of delivery of the accused to police, providing records, and participation in a civilian trial. In the facts of that case the Court found no actual conflict requiring the adjustment-rules route. The case is fact-specific; it does not abolish statutory protections in a case involving a genuine competing military forum claim.
Assessment: Create chronology of all military communications; Identify competent officer decisions and actual conduct; Record stage of court proceedings; Seek JAG analysis before contesting forum; Avoid retroactive characterisation of informal actions
Records: Police handover memo; Document requisitions; Trial witness records; Court orders
Red flags: Saying every absent notice invalidates civil trial; Ignoring prior intentional delivery to police
Illustration:

title: Custody under Army Act sections 101-103
body:
Command question: May a soldier be detained while facts are being checked?
Legal basis: Army Act ss 101-103
Legal position: The Army Act permits military custody under specified conditions and imposes command safeguards. Section 102 requires charge investigation or reasons for impracticability after 48 hours as calculated by the Act; section 103 requires repeated special reports when a non-active-service accused remains in custody without court-martial assembly. Military custody is not a substitute for unlimited informal detention.
Assessment: Confirm legal basis and command authority; Record exact start/time of custody; Apply section 102 calculation including express exclusions; Submit section 103 reports where triggered; Arrange counsel and procedural safeguards as applicable
Records: Custody order; Custody register; 48-hour calculation; Special reports
Red flags: Using arrest to pressure witnesses; Failing to track 48 hours; Treating police and military custody as interchangeable
Illustration:

title: Assistance from civil authorities
body:
Command question: When may police aid apprehension of a soldier?
Legal basis: Army Act ss 104-105
Legal position: Section 104 contemplates written commanding-officer applications for civilian assistance in apprehending a person subject to the Army Act accused of an offence under it. Section 105 addresses deserters and has its own information and apprehension arrangements. These provisions must be used for genuinely eligible persons and cannot substitute for lawful judicial processes.
Assessment: Confirm identity and jurisdiction; Prepare accurate written CO request; Coordinate with police and competent command; Preserve handover and medical/custody records; Avoid broad general searches or informal seizure demands
Records: Written application; Service-status proof; Police receipt; Handover memo
Red flags: Demanding arrest of civilian under Army Act; Omitting documentary basis; Treating desertion and AWOL identically
Illustration:

title: Police detention and handover
body:
Command question: Civil police have arrested a serving soldier: what follows?
Legal basis: Army Act ss 104-105,125-126; BNSS s 521
Legal position: Arrest by civilian police does not, by itself, resolve the trial forum. The unit should establish the precise offence, custody status, competent court stage and rights of the detainee; preserve communications and refer any jurisdiction question through the competent military and legal channels. Do not remove an accused from lawful police custody unilaterally.
Assessment: Confirm police station, FIR, legal grounds and custody; Provide necessary identity/official record assistance; Inform formation and JAG through proper channel; Identify any court notice and lawful forum mechanism; Record subsequent custody handover
Records: Arrest memo; FIR number; Custody handover; Competent authority communications
Red flags: Forcible unilateral custody transfer; Interference with investigation; Making an unverified promise of immunity
Illustration:

title: FIR reporting and police cooperation
body:
Command question: A cognisable offence may have occurred in cantonment: who investigates?
Legal basis: BNSS s 173 and applicable special law
Legal position: A cantonment or military workplace is not a blanket enclave free of ordinary criminal law. For a cognisable allegation, the competent police authority and criminal procedure must be considered; an internal inquiry should not be used to suppress or delay mandatory reporting. Police, military and specialist investigative roles may differ by offence and location.
Assessment: Secure immediate safety and medical attention; Document who received the complaint and when; Identify police reporting obligations without delay; Protect witnesses and evidence; Use JAG liaison for lawful document requests
Records: Initial report; FIR or police acknowledgement; Safety actions; Witness list
Red flags: Discouraging complainant from approaching police; Substituting CoI for mandatory criminal procedure; Destroying records
Illustration:

title: CoI versus civilian criminal investigation
body:
Command question: Can a CoI replace police investigation?
Legal basis: Army Rules 177-183; BNSS investigation provisions
Legal position: A Court of Inquiry is ordinarily an internal fact-finding mechanism and does not automatically oust the statutory powers of police or criminal courts. Where criminal misconduct is alleged, identify parallel obligations and ensure the CoI does not prejudice investigative rights, confidentiality or evidence integrity.
Assessment: Identify separate purposes and terms of reference; Record police case status; Coordinate permissible witness access; Avoid directing witnesses to harmonise accounts; Escalate conflict in evidence requests
Records: CoI convening order; Police status report; Evidence-access register; Written legal advice
Red flags: Calling CoI a criminal court; Withholding records solely due to internal inquiry; Contaminating witnesses
Illustration:

title: Chain of custody for weapons and objects
body:
Command question: How should a weapon or exhibit be handled after a civilian offence?
Legal basis: Evidence law and police seizure process
Legal position: Evidence reliability requires a traceable record of discovery, seizure, seals, storage, transfers and forensic dispatch. Service weapon registers and ammunition issue records may be relevant. The unit should preserve rather than recreate an evidentiary trail and should coordinate police access through lawful authorisation.
Assessment: Secure scene without altering evidence; Photograph and inventory exhibits; Record serials, seals and transfers; Preserve weapons and ammunition registers; Release seized items only against lawful recorded receipt
Records: Seal register; Weapon issue register; Seizure memo; Forensic receipt; Chain-of-custody log
Red flags: Cleaning or testing weapon without coordination; Backdating weapon issue; Unrecorded transfer
Illustration:

title: Electronic evidence and CCTV
body:
Command question: Can CCTV and chat messages be used as evidence?
Legal basis: BSA 2023, including s 1(2)
Legal position: The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam applies to judicial proceedings including courts-martial. Digital evidence can be important, but admissibility, authenticity, lawful acquisition and certificates depend on exact current provisions and facts. For a forensic handover preserve original data, metadata, extraction process, hashes and access logs rather than relying on screenshots alone.
Assessment: Secure original storage and avoid auto-overwrite; Record clocks and time-zone offsets; Create forensically controlled exports and hashes; Document access and device seizure; Have legal/forensic expert check evidence certificate requirements
Records: System log; Image hash; CCTV archive; Device owner record; Certificate where required
Red flags: Using cropped clip as only record; Unverifiable screenshots; Unlawful device search
Illustration:

title: Witness protection and fair procedure
body:
Command question: Can a superior officer instruct witnesses how to testify?
Legal basis: Constitutional fairness; evidence and military procedure
Legal position: Witness availability and protection are command responsibilities, but a commander cannot lawfully manufacture testimony or pressure persons to alter their account. Allegations concerning civilians or vulnerable persons require special protection and sensitive handling. An internal chain of command is not a substitute for independent police and judicial processes.
Assessment: Separate witnesses where practical and lawful; Record first report without coaching; Avoid repeated leading debriefings; Preserve communications and access logs; Refer protection requests through police/JAG
Records: Initial statements; Witness contact details held securely; Protection record; Duty roster
Red flags: Group rehearsals; Threats linked to posting/CR; Disclosure of protected identity
Illustration:

title: Requests for documents by police or court
body:
Command question: Must a unit give weapon logs and duty charts to police?
Legal basis: Police process, court orders and authorised information handling
Legal position: Official records may become material evidence. The unit should identify applicable lawful demands, classification or protective restrictions and competent disclosure authority, while ensuring court orders are respected. Classification must be addressed by lawful protective procedures, not used as an automatic reason to refuse an investigation.
Assessment: Log formal request and purpose; Preserve originals immediately; Consult competent disclosure/security authority; Supply certified extracts or seek lawful protective orders as appropriate; Record recipient and disclosure authority
Records: Request and order; Disclosure approval; Certified copies; Chain-of-custody record
Red flags: Unofficial unlogged handover; Destroying sensitive document; Automatic rejection citing secrecy
Illustration:

title: Arrested person's legal safeguards
body:
Command question: What must command do for a soldier held by police?
Legal basis: BNSS arrest/custody provisions; Army Act ss 101-103
Legal position: The applicable police arrest, production, legal representation and medical safeguards must be treated as distinct from military custody powers. The commander should establish welfare and legal liaison without directing police or witnesses improperly. Any detention or transfer requires the correct authority and documented legal route.
Assessment: Verify custody forum; Notify appropriate service authorities and family as permitted; Enable counsel contact through proper process; Preserve medical and handover record; Track every custody transition
Records: Arrest memo; Custody dates; Court order; Handover records
Red flags: Unofficial detention; Confusing command administration with police remand; Retaliation against complainant
Illustration:

title: Sudden, unnatural or suspicious death
body:
Command question: What should a CO do after an unexplained death at a unit?
Legal basis: BNSS ss 194,196
Legal position: BNSS section 194 covers police inquiry and reporting for suicide, accidental, homicidal and other suspicious deaths. Some categories may also engage magistrate inquiry under section 196. A military CoI may address service questions but cannot automatically replace the legally prescribed police, forensic, inquest and medical procedures.
Assessment: Secure life-saving assistance and scene; Inform competent civil authorities when legally required; Prevent evidence contamination; Maintain accurate family communication through proper channels; Convene internal inquiry only after distinguishing its remit
Records: Medical records; Scene log; Police inquest; Post-mortem documents; CoI terms; Family liaison record
Red flags: Premature cause-of-death conclusion; Removing body/evidence without authority; Internal inquiry used to block police
Illustration:

title: Fatal weapon discharge in barracks
body:
Command question: A service weapon has caused a fatality: what parallel tracks arise?
Legal basis: Army Act ss 69-70,125-126; BNSS ss 173,194
Legal position: A fatal shooting may engage a civilian crime, an Army offence, a death inquiry, weapon-accountability measures and service casualty reporting simultaneously. The law must first identify victim military status, alleged act, criminal forum and police investigation; no commander should assume that calling it an accidental discharge conclusively decides criminal liability.
Assessment: Obtain medical response and secure scene; Preserve weapon, ammunition and witnesses; Notify police/formation as required; Check s 70 victim-status implications; Obtain forum review through competent authority
Records: Weapon book; Ammunition tally; Medical inquest; Duty chart; FIR; CoI record
Red flags: Early declaration of accident; Cleaning gun; Manipulated issue record
Illustration:

title: Death during training or exercises
body:
Command question: What if a soldier or civilian dies during a training event?
Legal basis: BNSS ss 194,196; Army CoI
Legal position: Training fatalities call for prompt medical response, scene integrity, statutory death reporting, evidence preservation and separate service investigation into safety compliance. Liability and jurisdiction depend on events and persons rather than whether the activity was approved military training.
Assessment: Stop unsafe activity and assist casualties; Preserve orders, range logs and safety briefs; Engage police/inquest authorities as applicable; Record equipment state and video evidence; Separate fact findings from blame assignment
Records: Range safety orders; Training programme; Equipment logs; Medical records; Police record
Red flags: Restarting before evidence capture; Changing safety briefing retrospectively; Omitting civilian casualty investigation
Illustration:

title: Civilian injured by military vehicle
body:
Command question: A unit vehicle injures a pedestrian: what legal steps are relevant?
Legal basis: BNS/BNSS and Motor Vehicles Act where applicable
Legal position: Road accidents involving service vehicles may trigger ordinary criminal and civil compensation law and military administrative investigation. Status as a service driver does not confer automatic immunity; the precise offences, accident reporting obligations and compensation process require separate assessment.
Assessment: Arrange urgent medical aid and emergency services; Notify police and formation per rules; Preserve dashcam, vehicle log and driver duty records; Record public witnesses and scene conditions; Coordinate insurer/compensation offices where applicable
Records: Vehicle log; Driving authority; Accident site record; Police report; Medical records
Red flags: Moving vehicle to erase scene; Suppressing dashcam; Assuming service exemption from traffic law
Illustration:

title: Sexual offence involving civilian or dependent
body:
Command question: Can command resolve a serious sexual allegation through an internal inquiry?
Legal basis: Army Act s 70 and special criminal legislation
Legal position: Allegations of rape involving persons not subject to service law require immediate legal screening under section 70 and applicable civilian criminal protections. A CoI, mediation or command settlement cannot substitute for police and judicial requirements. Victim safety, confidentiality, medical care and protection from retaliation are immediate priorities.
Assessment: Ensure safety and access to medical care; Preserve confidential complaint and avoid repeated questioning; Identify statutory police reporting and jurisdiction; Prevent contact/retaliation where lawfully authorised; Refer to legal/specialist authorities without delay
Records: Initial report protected; Medical access record; Police acknowledgement; Protection instructions
Red flags: Pressuring withdrawal; Treating consent or settlement as reason not to report; Disclosing protected identity
Illustration:

title: Allegation involving a minor
body:
Command question: What changes when the affected person is below 18?
Legal basis: POCSO Act 2012, BNS, BNSS, Army Act
Legal position: Child protection law may impose specific mandatory reporting and investigation safeguards. The unit should not interview children as though conducting an ordinary service inquiry or disclose identities widely. A court-martial versus civilian trial analysis must account for special-statute requirements and competent investigative authorities.
Assessment: Protect child immediately; Alert mandated authorities promptly under verified law; Restrict access to identifying information; Avoid repeated amateur interviews; Coordinate specialist victim-support pathway
Records: Protected report; Authority acknowledgement; Restricted-access evidence register
Red flags: No-report compromise; Identity disclosure; Improper interview by command
Illustration:

title: Loss/theft of weapon linked to civilian crime
body:
Command question: What if a service weapon is missing and used outside?
Legal basis: Army Rule 185; BNS/BNSS and Arms Act
Legal position: Loss or theft of military weapons may raise both service-accountability questions and ordinary criminal investigation, including public-safety concerns. The special higher-authority inquiry provisions and current service instructions must be verified; police reporting or investigative action cannot be displaced by a routine inventory Board alone.
Assessment: Secure armoury and reconcile stock; Notify authorised chain and civil authorities as required; Record last custody and issue; Preserve access logs and CCTV; Separate evidence recovery from accountability findings
Records: Armoury ledger; Issue book; CCTV; Incident report; Police FIR
Red flags: Using routine stock adjustment to conceal loss; Unrecorded weapon recovery
Illustration:

title: Death or injury in military custody
body:
Command question: A detainee is seriously injured while held by the unit: what is required?
Legal basis: Army Act ss 101-103; BNSS ss 194,196 and custody safeguards
Legal position: Custodial injury or death demands immediate medical and legally required investigative responses. The unit must not treat service disciplinary secrecy as a substitute for statutory death/custody inquiries or legitimate external oversight. Preserve custody register, observations, medical examinations, CCTV and communications.
Assessment: Arrange emergency treatment; Notify required authorities and legal chain; Preserve cell and custody records; Protect witnesses from intimidation; Obtain immediate independent legal advice
Records: Custody orders; Medical exams; CCTV; Duty roster; Police/magistrate record
Red flags: Delay in reporting; Altering custody book; Unlawful deprivation of liberty

title: Incident beyond India
body:
Command question: What if a soldier commits an alleged civilian offence abroad?
Legal basis: Army Act ss 69-70,124; BNS s 1
Legal position: Army Act section 69 can extend to civil offences committed outside India, with the statutory section 70 exception framework. Host-state jurisdiction, status-of-forces arrangements, diplomatic obligations and applicable local or international law may separately govern. No single unilateral court-martial conclusion is appropriate without specialist legal consultation.
Assessment: Confirm location and timeline; Check host law/treaty and command deployment basis; Preserve consular/diplomatic notifications; Screen Army Act jurisdiction; Seek Army HQ/JAG direction before forum or custody action
Records: Deployment orders; Status agreement; Incident location proof; Host police documents
Red flags: Assuming automatic immunity abroad; Ignoring host authority; Unapproved diplomatic communications

title: 1 July 2024 law transition
body:
Command question: Which criminal statute applies to an incident spanning June and July 2024?
Legal basis: BNS s 358; BNSS s 531
Legal position: The replacement of IPC, CrPC and the Evidence Act in 2024 requires distinct treatment of offence dates, pending proceedings and evidentiary rules. BNS section 358 and BNSS section 531 contain savings. The unit must not automatically replace every historic IPC reference with a current BNS section or assume the procedural act for a pre-transition pending case.
Assessment: Identify exact alleged act date; Record investigation/inquiry pendency on 1 July 2024; Read savings and Gazette commencement; Map old and new provisions by elements not numbering; Seek specialist legal validation
Records: Offence chronology; First FIR; Court filing timeline; Applicable gazette notice
Red flags: Retrospective charge based on new section; Mechanical statute number substitution; Ignoring pending-investigation saving

title: BNSS section 521 and former CrPC section 475
body:
Command question: How does court-martial delivery work under new criminal procedure?
Legal basis: BNSS s 521; former CrPC s 475
Legal position: BNSS section 521 provides for Central Government rules governing trial forum allocation and delivery to military commanding officers in appropriate cases. The 1978 adjustment rules refer to the former CrPC and should be read only with authenticated current legal continuity/adaptation materials. The application must display a date-and-version gate.
Assessment: Check proceedings started before or after 1 July 2024; Read s 521 current text; Locate current valid Government adjustment rules; Identify Magistrate stage and written notices; Refer uncertain legal continuity to JAG
Records: Statutory excerpts; Gazette rule version; Magistrate order; Authority response
Red flags: Using CrPC 475 text as automatic 2026 law; Assuming BNSS 521 alone grants CO forum-choice power

title: BSA applies to courts-martial
body:
Command question: Does new evidence law bind a court-martial?
Legal basis: BSA s 1(2)
Legal position: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam section 1(2) expressly extends the Act to judicial proceedings in or before Courts, including courts-martial. The relevant commencement and savings rules, the Army Act evidence provisions and court-martial procedure must be analysed together for a particular case.
Assessment: Find trial date and applicable law; Check Army Act evidence-specific provisions; Identify statutory rules on electronic records; Examine authenticity and collection chain; Refer to judge advocate for admissibility issues
Records: Evidence list; Proposed exhibits; Electronic certificates; Trial chronology
Red flags: Assuming BSA irrelevant to military courts; Applying ordinary rules without considering special Act; Unexamined electronic files

title: Jurisdiction if military authority does not elect trial
body:
Command question: Is a civilian court barred because no military forum decision was made?
Legal basis: State of Sikkim v Jasbir Singh paras 44-47
Legal position: The Supreme Court explains that the section 125 choice must be exercised by a competent authority; non-exercise does not itself strip an ordinary criminal court of inherent competence in concurrent-jurisdiction cases. Actual handover, cooperation and litigation conduct can be highly relevant.
Assessment: Identify whether forum election was made; Examine evidence of deliberate handover; Check court procedural stage; Distinguish genuine contest from unilateral late objection; Record legal conclusions and relevant paragraphs
Records: Forum election order; Handover memo; Police requisitions; Trial status
Red flags: Trying to invalidate a criminal trial on an automatic jurisdiction theory

title: Sanctions and claims of special immunity
body:
Command question: Do AFSPA or official duty automatically bar investigation?
Legal basis: Special statutes and controlling judgments; context specific
Legal position: Requirements for prior sanction arise only under the relevant law and facts, including the relationship of alleged conduct to official duties and the area/operation. There is no universal rule that all service personnel or alleged acts are immune from police investigation or criminal trial. Special statute claims need urgent competent JAG review.
Assessment: Identify exact statute and notification; Identify area and incident date; Record duty and operation; Distinguish investigation from prosecution and cognizance; Do not prevent lawful investigative steps without court protection
Records: Deployment orders; Area notification; Duty log; Sanction correspondence
Red flags: Blanket immunity claim; Ignoring serious allegation; Treating public commentary as competent legal opinion

title: Preservation of constitutional rights
body:
Command question: How are fair trial and liberty rights protected in concurrent forums?
Legal basis: Constitution Articles 20-22; Army Act and BNSS safeguards
Legal position: Military and civilian process remain governed by constitutional constraints and applicable safeguards. The service setting does not permit arbitrary confinement, compelled self-incrimination, fabrication or retaliatory action. Consult case-specific rules where Article 33 modifications for Armed Forces may be relevant.
Assessment: Preserve arrest, charge and legal-access history; Track delays and reasons; Review independent court orders; Ensure no coercion of witness/accused; Seek prompt JAG advice when rights conflict
Records: Custody register; Legal notices; Charge sheet; Medical record
Red flags: Threats or compelled admissions; Ignoring judicial directions; Assuming all civilian rights disappear in Army

title: First-hour incident response
body:
Command question: What should a commander do during the first hour of a potentially criminal incident?
Legal basis: Unit safety duty and applicable offence/custody law
Legal position: Priority is to preserve life, prevent ongoing harm, secure the scene and notify competent authorities. A prompt factual incident log is more valuable than premature conclusions about guilt, forum or blame. Where police attendance or mandatory reporting is required it should not be delayed for an internal Court of Inquiry.
Assessment: Arrange emergency help; Isolate hazards while preserving evidence; Capture initial facts and time; Inform authorised civil and military authorities; Avoid interviews that taint witness testimony
Records: Time log; Medical calls; Scene record; Police contact acknowledgement
Red flags: Premature label of accident; Removing evidence; Delaying external authority reporting

title: Competent authority and delegation audit
body:
Command question: How should the assistant identify who is empowered to act?
Legal basis: Army Act ss 125-126; current orders/delegations
Legal position: Command responsibilities and legally conferred powers are distinct. Authority to secure and report an incident is not necessarily authority to choose court-martial, impose punishment, withhold a police record or decide prosecution sanction. The system must require exact appointment, delegated instrument, effective dates and verification.
Assessment: List proposed legal action; Map to precise enabling provision; Identify office and delegation; Check validity on event/decision date; Block unsupported automated approvals
Records: Appointment order; Warrant/delegation; Policy version; JAG verification
Red flags: Using a rank title alone as proof of power; Invented delegation; Outdated warrant

title: Civil authority communications register
body:
Command question: What correspondence should be recorded with police and Magistrates?
Legal basis: Court jurisdiction and public record integrity
Legal position: Maintain auditable incoming and outgoing records for FIR requests, summons, handover, seizure, jurisdiction notices and compliance. Preserve original wording and delivery timestamps, and restrict modifications. The register supports later adjudication of forum choice and the unit’s cooperation.
Assessment: Register every communication and reference ID; Log date and lawful authority; Attach exact scans and hashes; Track response deadline and completion; Review overdue escalations daily
Records: Dispatch/receipt log; Police letters; Court orders; Digital hashes
Red flags: Lost notice or email; Undated oral instruction; Unauthorised disclosure

title: Source hierarchy and currency gate
body:
Command question: What if a handbook contradicts current statute or binding judgment?
Legal basis: Statutory supremacy and judicial precedent
Legal position: The assistant must prioritise authenticated legislation and binding court holdings over publisher commentary, internal notes or older secondary sources. A 1978 procedural citation must be version-gated following 2024 criminal-law replacement. If the present authoritative instrument is unavailable, the application must abstain from a definitive procedural order.
Assessment: Identify exact contested issue; Retrieve statute effective on event date; Retrieve current notification and judgment treatment; Compare against internal policy only within legal competence; Record reviewer decision
Records: Source version; Gazette amendment; Case citation; Legal reviewer approval
Red flags: Confident but uncited answers; Treating quoted headline as law; Obsolete IPC/CrPC procedures

title: Decision report and close-out
body:

Legal basis: Command records, court orders and source validation
Legal position: A command legal file should present verified facts, unresolved questions, legal alternatives, exact authority and chronology without prejudging guilt. Follow-up orders and documents should be stored with review dates. Case closure depends on lawful disposition and record retention, not merely completing an internal board.
Assessment: Prepare chronology and allegation matrix; Index source documents and chain of custody; Record JAG advice and competent decision; Track criminal and service proceedings separately; Close with preserved audit trail and access controls
Records: Chronology; Decision sheet; JAG opinion; Police and CoI outcomes; Compliance record
Red flags: Unclear forum status; Misplaced original evidence; Invented approval

title: Map the legal forum before applying evidence rules
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: The BSA expressly covers judicial proceedings including courts-martial. A CoI and a Summary of Evidence are earlier and distinct military processes; their own statutory and rule-based treatment must be followed. Evidence taken at either stage does not simply become trial evidence because a copy exists.

ASSESSMENT: Identify CoI, SoE, SCM, GCM/DCM/SGCM or civilian court | confirm legal status and dates | identify governing statute and specific rule | preserve procedural record separately from trial exhibit register

RECORDS: Convening order | charge sheet | SoE | CoI proceedings | trial order

RISKS: Treating a CoI as criminal court | assuming earlier testimony automatically proves a charge
references: BSA s1(2); Army Act s133; Army Rules RR177,182

title: Distinguish pre-July 2024 proceedings
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: Section 170 repeals the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, while preserving its application to specified matters pending immediately before commencement. The relevant question is not merely when the allegation arose, but the status and commencement of the particular application, trial, inquiry, investigation, proceeding or appeal. Apply a documented transitional analysis.

ASSESSMENT: Record incident date | record dates of each proceeding and whether pending before 1 July 2024 | document savings provision decision | request legal opinion in mixed or reopened cases

RECORDS: First order | registration dates | procedural chronology | legal opinion

RISKS: Applying BSA only based on incident date | silently changing section numbers

title: Resolve Army Act s133 legacy reference
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: The 2025 Army Act consolidation still refers to the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 in section 133. The later BSA expressly applies to courts-martial. The operative interaction needs statutory interpretation and current authenticated amendment review. A research assistant must expose the apparent cross-reference rather than claim the text was amended.

ASSESSMENT: Display both texts and dates | identify law applicable to pending matter | request JAG interpretative review | show verified section language before advice

RECORDS: Authenticated statutes | review note | Gazette amendment search

RISKS: Inventing an amendment to s133 | suppressing older citation | applying BSA to saved proceedings without analysis

LEGAL REVIEW: LEGAL_AUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED
references: Army Act s133; BSA ss1 and170

title: Separate evidentiary admissibility, relevance and weight
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: Evidence may be relevant yet require an independent mode of proof before admission. Even an admitted exhibit can have low probative value because of identification, authenticity, contamination, inconsistent testimony or weak chain of custody. Treat these as separate decisions.

ASSESSMENT: Identify fact in issue | test relevance | decide method of proof | identify authenticity source | evaluate credibility and corroboration

RECORDS: Evidence matrix | exhibit register | witness list | admissibility objections

RISKS: Using the word evidence as proof of truth | assuming admissibility equals guilt

title: Identify burden of proof and relevant exceptions
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: The general burden rests on the party asserting facts necessary to obtain judgment and, in criminal prosecution, ordinarily on the prosecution to establish its case to the applicable standard. Specific statutory exceptions and facts especially within knowledge require precise legal analysis; they do not provide a shortcut around foundational proof.

ASSESSMENT: Set out elements of each charge | map prosecution evidence to every element | map legal exceptions | assess defence and contrary evidence separately

RECORDS: Charge-elements matrix | evidence chart | expert evidence

RISKS: Demanding accused prove innocence | shifting burden without identifying provision

title: Conduct examination-in-chief and cross-examination
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: Examination-in-chief establishes a witness account. Cross-examination tests it; re-examination clarifies matters raised. For military trial, comply additionally with the Army Rules on presence, recording, witness procedure and defence opportunities. Never manufacture certainty by coaching a witness to match another statement.

ASSESSMENT: Confirm witness competence and language | elicit first-hand account | allow lawful cross-examination | record answers and objections | document translation and corrections

RECORDS: Witness list | recorded Q and A | translations | objections

RISKS: Leading a material witness improperly | excluding defence questions | combining separate accounts

title: Recognise leading questions
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: The BSA differentiates leading questions in examination-in-chief and re-examination from cross-examination. Subject to exceptions and the court permission, disputed material facts should be elicited without suggesting the desired answer. Administrative investigators should similarly avoid shaping testimony.

ASSESSMENT: Draft open factual questions | record exact witness response | ask who what where when how | identify where leading question permission is needed

RECORDS: Question plan | transcript | reasons for corrections

RISKS: Making witnesses repeat suggested answers | filling gaps with investigator theory

title: Previous statements and contradiction
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: A prior written statement may be used in cross-examination in accordance with statutory requirements. The CoI exception in Rule 182 permits use of CoI proceedings for cross-examination but does not convert the whole inquiry into substantive proof against the person. Precisely identify which passage is relied upon.

ASSESSMENT: Preserve original prior statement | identify page and passage | put material inconsistency with appropriate legal foundation | preserve answer | assess its significance

RECORDS: Prior signed statement | transcript | exact page/line index

RISKS: Reading entire CoI file as substantive evidence | omitting opportunity to explain discrepancy

title: Witness competence and communication accommodation
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: Witnesses may be competent notwithstanding age or inability to communicate verbally; the governing law requires a case-specific assessment. The record should establish how the person understood questions and how answers were accurately communicated, including language interpretation where necessary.

ASSESSMENT: Identify language and communication requirements | document interpreter | avoid unrecorded paraphrase | seek procedural direction for vulnerable witness

RECORDS: Interpreter record | testimony record | method of communication

RISKS: Treating minor or non-verbal witness as automatically incompetent | inaccurate translation

title: Respect privilege, official secrecy and protected material
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: The law protects defined confidential communications and imposes conditions on production of official records. Military operational classification alone does not decide every evidentiary question, and a witness-summons power does not eliminate statutory privileges. Seek an authorised determination before disclosure.

ASSESSMENT: Identify classification | identify asserted privilege | refer to competent authority/legal adviser | record any court order | preserve both redacted and source record securely

RECORDS: Privilege log | document inventory | authority record | access register

RISKS: Automatic disclosure of secret document | reflexively withholding without legal basis

title: Assess a witness unavailable at the preliminary stage
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: Rule 23 contains a limited method for incorporating a signed witness statement where attendance at the Summary of Evidence cannot readily be procured and the prescribed certificate is made. That is not automatic permission to avoid witness attendance at a later court-martial; the court must apply the applicable law.

ASSESSMENT: Document efforts to secure attendance | record lawful reason and certificate | provide statement to accused as required | separately plan attendance or commission for trial

RECORDS: Witness request | certification | statement | summons

RISKS: Substituting unsigned officer summary | invoking expediency without reasons

title: Summons and commissions
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: Section 135 confers defined summons powers, with safeguards and limits. Sections 137-138 provide mechanisms for examining a witness on commission where ordinary attendance would entail unreasonable delay, cost or inconvenience. Do not assume every CoI officer can compel a civilian witness.

ASSESSMENT: Identify stage and officer with statutory power | identify witness/material | issue proper summons | assess impossibility and commission route | track service and compliance

RECORDS: Signed summons | proof of service | witness response | commission correspondence

RISKS: Wrong authority issuing notice | coercing civilian attendance without power

title: Avoid witness intimidation and tainted testimony
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: Procedural integrity requires that witnesses are not pressured, rewarded for a preferred account or made to review other witnesses narratives. A unit should record potential conflicts of interest and preserve independent first reports. Any allegation of interference requires early legal and command reporting.

ASSESSMENT: Secure first-hand account promptly | separate witnesses where justified | document access | log threats or interference | escalate concerns

RECORDS: First report | interview log | interference report

RISKS: Witness coaching | group interview before first statement | retaliatory treatment

title: Court of Inquiry evidence is ordinarily non-admissible against subject
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: Rule 182 provides a specific restriction on admission of CoI proceedings, confessions, statements and answers against a person subject to the Army Act, subject to statutory exceptions including use for cross-examination and proceedings for wilful false evidence. Thus a CoI is a fact-finding and command decision input, not a substitute for prosecutorial proof.

ASSESSMENT: Label CoI material separately | apply admissibility restriction | preserve for lawful cross-examination | collect independently admissible evidence for trial

RECORDS: CoI file | witness originals | provenance records | prosecution evidence plan

RISKS: Simply annexing CoI as proof of guilt | treating findings as a conviction

title: Rule 180 opportunity when reputation affected
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: When an inquiry affects a person’s character or military reputation, Rule 180 provides participation safeguards including presence, statement, evidence and appropriate cross-examination. These safeguards must be assessed when a new adverse allegation emerges during an inquiry, not only on initial convening.

ASSESSMENT: Check testimony as it develops | identify affected person | document notice and participation | record any adjournment and opportunity | obtain advice if already partly concluded

RECORDS: Notice | attendance | questions | witness record

RISKS: Failing to revisit Rule 180 after facts change | assuming retrospective paper notice always cures

title: Summary of Evidence rights and scope
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: The SoE is a written evidentiary record taken in the presence and hearing of the accused in the manner of Rule 23. The accused may cross-examine, make a voluntary statement after appropriate caution, and call defence witnesses; evidence must be read over and signed as provided. This is a preliminary stage and the later trial has its own evidentiary safeguards.

ASSESSMENT: Check hearing stage and authorisation | record witnesses in presence of accused | capture questions and answers | caution accused | read/translate record | facilitate defence witnesses

RECORDS: Rule 22 proceedings | SoE | signatures | translations

RISKS: Excluding defence witness | omission of cross-examination | using coerced statement

title: Summary of Evidence is not sworn trial evidence
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: The Ministry of Defence-hosted explanatory notes state that a SoE is not taken on oath or affirmation. Its treatment during trial is regulated, including use of a prior statement for legitimate contradiction. The court must receive evidence according to applicable trial requirements rather than treat the SoE as the default witness testimony.

ASSESSMENT: Separate SoE witness versions from trial transcripts | verify oath/affirmation procedure at trial | plan witness production | document specific permitted use of prior statements

RECORDS: SoE | trial Q and A | witness summons

RISKS: Accepting SoE transcript as complete substantive evidence | swearing SoE contrary to procedure

title: Court-Martial witness production and surprise evidence
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: Army Rules provide for prosecution witnesses and notice where a witness is called whose evidence was not included in the summary provided to accused. The purpose is not merely record completeness but effective opportunity to meet that evidence. The application should flag late witnesses and recommend procedural legal review.

ASSESSMENT: Compare trial witness list to disclosed SoE | identify new witness | provide required advance notice and abstract | record any adjournment | preserve decision

RECORDS: Disclosed witness list | notice | abstract of proposed evidence | court order

RISKS: Ambush witness | withholding material from defence | reliance on unexplained new testimony

title: Preserve scene and physical exhibit provenance
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: Photographs, fragments, weapons, damaged equipment and clothing can support or contradict an account. Collection and custody should be documented from discovery to examination and production. A chain-of-custody log is an evidentiary safeguard and good practice; it is not a standalone universal statutory formula whose breach automatically decides admissibility.

ASSESSMENT: Isolate scene safely | photograph before movement | allocate exhibit ID | log collector/location/time | secure transfer | obtain expert report | document access

RECORDS: Scene log | photographs | exhibit tags | transfer log | tamper seals

RISKS: Unlabelled exhibits | undocumented transfer | cleaning or modifying evidence before documentation

title: Distinguish primary and secondary documents
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: The BSA defines primary evidence and enumerates forms of secondary evidence and conditions for their use. An authenticated certified copy, photocopy or digital scan is not categorically equivalent to the original for every fact. Determine the proper means to prove each disputed document.

ASSESSMENT: Identify document origin | locate original | record why not produced | check certified copy status | determine statutory mode of proof

RECORDS: Original/copy log | certification | notice-to-produce record

RISKS: Treating every scanned letter as original | introducing unauthenticated copy without legal foundation

title: Official records, public documents and certified copies
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: Service registers, medical records, orders and disciplinary registers may require different routes to proof, including relevant public-document and certified-copy provisions. Confidentiality, redaction and assertions of privilege require independent consideration. A unit clerk is not automatically a legally competent certifying authority for every document.

ASSESSMENT: Identify custodian | verify document category | obtain proper certification | preserve complete version | log disclosure authority

RECORDS: Original records | certified copy | certification order | release record

RISKS: Mislabeling privately held letter as public record | unofficial stamp on inaccurate extract

title: Prepare exhibit list linked to the charge elements
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: A reliable exhibit register maps each item to the exact proposition it is relied upon to establish. For every element of a charge, identify witness, exhibit and any gap or contrary material. The presence of many exhibits cannot compensate for absence of proof of an essential legal element.

ASSESSMENT: Enumerate elements | attach item ID | record relevant fact | identify collector and authenticating witness | identify objections

RECORDS: Proof matrix | exhibit register | charge sheet

RISKS: Conflating possession with use | failing to prove identity of person/device

title: Apply BSA electronic-record framework
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: The BSA recognises electronic and digital records and treats them as documentary evidence when statutory conditions are met. Section 61 bars refusal merely because of digital form, but explicitly operates subject to section 63. Section 57 also recognises certain multi-file and proper-custody electronic records as primary evidence. These provisions must be read together.

ASSESSMENT: Identify original device/file | distinguish direct original from derived output | establish lawful custody | apply section 63 conditions as required | record integrity checks

RECORDS: Device inventory | original image | source metadata | certificate | chain log

RISKS: Believing section 61 eliminates section 63 | calling every screenshot primary

title: Section 63 certification and Schedule
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: Section 63(4) specifies a certificate to accompany the electronic record at each instance of submission for admission, addressing identification, manner of production, device particulars and statutory conditions; the scheduled form includes party and expert portions. Preparation of a certificate must reflect actual facts about the source system. False or boilerplate statements create serious risk.

ASSESSMENT: Identify signatories and factual knowledge | complete relevant Schedule fields | link to hash/source ID | certify each tender as required | obtain legal assessment if original device produced

RECORDS: BSA Schedule certificate | device details | hash log | acquisition report

RISKS: Copying an old Evidence Act 65B certificate blindly | claiming knowledge the signer lacks | omitting expert role

title: Preserve CCTV and access-control recordings
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: Video evidence depends on camera identification, timestamps, time-sync errors, retention windows, export process, continuity and possible editing. The safest approach preserves the native recording and a documented read-only working copy as early as possible, while minimising ordinary reuse of the recording device.

ASSESSMENT: Identify DVR/NVR | note system clock deviation | export native format and player where needed | hash | seal working copy | preserve custodian affidavit/certificate

RECORDS: Camera map | DVR logs | export manifest | checksums | Section 63 papers

RISKS: Overwritten footage | phone-filming a monitor as sole record | undocumented transcoding

title: Preserve mobile messages, calls and photographs
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: A chat screenshot may omit surrounding messages, sender identity, delivery metadata and account/device context. Preserve the device or properly acquired record within lawful authority and make only supported claims about who controlled or used an account. For official systems, avoid importing private material without a valid legal basis.

ASSESSMENT: Record lawful authority/consent or direction | isolate source | preserve contextual conversation and metadata | record extraction method | test account attribution

RECORDS: Device and account details | extraction log | certificate | contact/metadata corroboration

RISKS: Identifying sender only from display name | cropped screenshot | unauthorised search

title: Hash verification and immutable preservation
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: A cryptographic hash assists in demonstrating that two byte sequences are identical. It does not independently prove who created the file, whether the recording is true, or whether the recording device clock was accurate. Record SHA-256 of acquired files and recheck on transfers; preserve original unmodified bytes.

ASSESSMENT: Calculate SHA-256 on acquisition | store manifest separately | rehash on handover | maintain read-only evidence | disclose any mismatch and investigate

RECORDS: SHA-256 manifest | custodian log | acquisition time | tool version

RISKS: Asserting hash proves content truth | hashing after undocumented edits | treating re-encoded video as same original

title: Understand historical electronic-evidence case law
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: These decisions construed Section 65B of the repealed Indian Evidence Act and explained certificates and original-device distinction. They are essential background, but not substitutes for close reading of BSA s63, including changed wording and the statutory Schedule. Verify how subsequent judgments apply old reasoning to the new framework.

ASSESSMENT: Identify whether proceeding is governed by old IEA or BSA | read ratio and material facts | compare statutory text | verify later treatment | apply to specific evidence type

RECORDS: Judgment extract | BSA-IEA comparison | case-specific opinion

RISKS: Applying pre-2024 language as a verbatim BSA rule | alleging original always dispenses with all documentation
references: Arjun Panditrao Khotkar (2020); Anvar P V (2014)

title: Objections to method of proving electronic material
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: The historical Supreme Court decision discusses timing of mode-of-proof objections and waiver of curable formal defects. It does not authorise fabrication of a missing certificate or elimination of BSA requirements. The application should record when and on what basis the objection was raised and recommend legal review.

ASSESSMENT: Record tender date and objections | identify whether issue is intrinsic admissibility or mode of proof | preserve court decision | seek review before any late objection

RECORDS: Tender log | objection text | exhibit admission record

RISKS: Assuming all failures to object mean evidence is unquestionably authentic

title: Air-gapped systems: logs, exports and authority
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: On isolated LAN systems, the audit trail may include local Windows logs, server records, access logs, signed events, CCTV and time-service configuration. Maintain separate records of acquisition permissions and technical provenance. A lack of internet time-sync may create clock drift; it does not make evidence inherently useless.

ASSESSMENT: Identify system owner | preserve log originals and timezone | capture time offsets | export in native format | hash | log access and software versions

RECORDS: System clock evidence | event logs | export script | hashes | authorisation

RISKS: Clearing logs during troubleshooting | confusing UTC with IST | editing production DB records

title: Drone, sensor and simulator telemetry
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: Mission logs, command histories, frame captures and software telemetry may corroborate an incident, but require a validated account of sensor calibration, firmware, processing and timestamps. Distinguish raw capture from AI inference, and preserve inputs and model/version where an automated conclusion is advanced.

ASSESSMENT: Identify sensor and version | capture native files | record system calibration | preserve model/algorithm version | obtain qualified expert explanation | log uncertainty

RECORDS: Native telemetry | configuration | firmware version | calibration report | analysis log

RISKS: Treating AI-generated label as witnessed fact | losing processing provenance | importing training data
references: BSA ss57,61-63; BSA s39 expert opinion

title: Maintain lawful access and information security
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: A legal assistant handling operational evidence must not release classified or personal records beyond authorised persons. Data minimisation, sealed case workspaces, audit trails and role-based access are necessary design controls. The precise legal authority for device search, disclosure and retention is case- and organisation-specific.

ASSESSMENT: Check authority for collection | apply classification marking | limit access by role | keep immutable activity log | obtain authority before external disclosure

RECORDS: Access approval | classification decision | audit log | retention schedule

RISKS: Uploading classified evidence to external service | using private phone for investigation images
references: BSA ss129-136; Army Act s136; applicable service policies

title: Expert opinion is relevant but not conclusive
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: Expert opinion may assist with technical, medical, scientific, handwriting or forensic issues. Courts must consider qualifications, methodology, data, assumptions, quality checks and alternative explanations. An expert opinion cannot supply missing factual provenance or cure loss of the underlying source data.

ASSESSMENT: Document expert qualifications | supply original material securely | ask narrow questions | obtain methodology and limitations | seek rebuttal opportunity

RECORDS: Expert CV | laboratory chain log | report | raw results

RISKS: Treating a consultant assertion as certain | withholding unfavourable error margins

title: Medical, injury and post-mortem evidence
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: A medical finding should be separated from eyewitness description and legal conclusions. A medical officer may explain injury mechanism, time ranges and limitations; the investigator must not convert an approximate medical estimate into a precise account unsupported by evidence. Preserve examination and sample provenance.

ASSESSMENT: Record injury and custody timelines | identify examiner | preserve original report and sample labels | note uncertainty | obtain expert testimony as required

RECORDS: MLC | post-mortem | sample seals | lab reports

RISKS: Concluding cause and intent solely from injury | ignoring handling of samples

title: Forensic image and audio authentication
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: Cropped images, compressed videos and extracted audio can be edited inadvertently during routine use. Examiners should record tool versions, sample handling, transformations and all assumptions. A probabilistic voice or face analysis is not interchangeable with definitive identity proof.

ASSESSMENT: Preserve native file | hash | record every transformation | retain analysis project | independently corroborate identity | disclose uncertainty

RECORDS: Originals | metadata | processing log | validation report

RISKS: Presenting edited media as original | invented certainty from face recognition

title: Protect the accused right to prepare a defence
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: Disclosure, adequate preparation time and opportunity to test witness evidence are essential to an effective defence. Military trial orders must be scrutinised in context, and late evidence may require notice or adjournment. The application should flag failures for legal assessment rather than pronounce automatic invalidity.

ASSESSMENT: Verify charge and SoE availability | document preparation time | track requests for witnesses | flag undisclosed witnesses | record adjournment application

RECORDS: Disclosure receipt | witness requests | court record

RISKS: Ambush evidence | discouraging defence witness | withholding source document

title: Record evidence faithfully and preserve corrections
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: Accuracy of the written record is itself an evidentiary safeguard. Record questions and answers, interpret where necessary, read back applicable statements and make visible corrections with signatures rather than silently overwriting a disputed answer. The record must show who observed or authenticated any correction.

ASSESSMENT: Take verbatim material answer | review with witness | mark correction | date and sign | retain original version where appropriate

RECORDS: Signed transcript | correction audit | interpreter note

RISKS: Retrospective clean copy changing words | unsupported inserted statement

title: Avoid treating adverse evidence as a finding of guilt
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: Even where an inquiry or an expert report suggests misconduct, legal liability depends on each element of the charge and applicable standard of proof. An inculpatory fact must be assessed together with exculpatory facts and alternative explanations. A command briefing should identify facts, allegations and findings separately.

ASSESSMENT: Separate proven facts from allegations | list every charge element | identify contradictions | refer disputed determinations to trial forum

RECORDS: Proof matrix | chronology | material contradictions

RISKS: Prejudging trial in CoI findings | suppressing defence evidence

title: Create a legal-review checkpoint for device seizure and disclosure
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: Possession of a military device or workplace access does not automatically confer authority to search all accounts or export personal data. Investigators should determine lawful process, scope and necessity before access; an evidentiary need does not override privilege, classified handling or fundamental rights.

ASSESSMENT: Identify authorised investigator | document grounds and scope | obtain warranted approvals | segregate privileged material | plan lawful disclosure

RECORDS: Approval | acquisition scope | privilege screen | access register

RISKS: Unauthorized full-device imaging | cloud upload | blanket disclosure of personal records
references: BSA ss57-63; Army Act s136; service authority instruments

title: AI-assisted analysis is not independent evidence
body:
CORE PRINCIPLE: LLM-generated summaries, speech transcripts, auto-captioned videos and AI detections are processing outputs. They can help search and organise source material but require separate provenance, corroboration and human review. A model conclusion is not a witness statement or forensic expert report simply because it appears plausible.

ASSESSMENT: Retain source file | identify model and prompt/version | compare output to original | have qualified person validate | cite original not model text

RECORDS: Raw source | transformation manifest | reviewer sign-off

RISKS: Invented quotes | hallucinated timestamps | automated credibility scoring

title: Electronic-record certificate intake
body:
UNAPPROVED RESEARCH FORMAT
Case; output ID; BSA s63/IEA s65B governing law; BSA Schedule Part A and B fields as applicable; person in charge and expert credentials; signatory basis; time/date of each tender.

title: Witness inconsistency register
body:
UNAPPROVED RESEARCH FORMAT
Witness; first statement date; earlier passage and page; later passage; exact inconsistency; opportunity for explanation; rule invoked; court decision.

title: Exhibit-to-element matrix
body:
UNAPPROVED RESEARCH FORMAT
Each charge element; prosecution witness; exhibit IDs; specific proposition; proof route; contradictory material; missing proof; JAG review status.

title: Expert referral brief
body:
UNAPPROVED RESEARCH FORMAT
Questions requiring expert assessment; source files and hashes; collection/storage chain; scientific method requested; need to state limitations; confidentiality and return requirements.

title: CoI-to-trial evidentiary segregation sheet
body:
UNAPPROVED RESEARCH FORMAT
CoI title and date; person affected; Rule 180 action; CoI materials restricted under Rule 182; independent corroborating evidence; Rule 182 exception use, if any; disclosure log.

title: Evidence integrity incident report
body:
UNAPPROVED RESEARCH FORMAT
Discovery date/time; lost/modified item; last verified hash/custodian; affected copies; immediate stop measures; containment; independent investigation; reporting authority; legal decision.
